articles.title: Putin Signs a Decree Increasing Russian Army: Over 2.4 Million, Including 1.5 Million Active-Duty Personnel
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree on Monday, Sept. 28, increasing the size of Russia’s armed forces to 2.4 million, including 1.5 million active-duty military personnel.
The document, No. 700, was published on Russia’s official legal information portal, marking the fourth time such a decree was signed this year, according to Russian state-owned media TASS.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The document also instructs the Russian government to allocate the federal budget funds that the Russian Defense Ministry needs to carry out the increase.
The announcement comes as President Volodymyr Zelensky warned earlier on Monday that Russia has already begun additional mobilization and is expanding its use of North Korean troops, with over 8,000 already in Russia and up to 50,000 more planned.
Nearly 50,000 more since march
The new ceiling is 15,500 higher than the one set in a decree that took effect on Aug. 1, which put the military at 2,426,130 personnel, including 1,535,000 troops.
In March, a presidential decree set the total at 2,391,770, and a June decree raised it to 2,399,130.
Overall, the authorized size of Russia’s military has grown by 49,860 since March, according to TASS.
Kyiv Post has not independently verified these numbers.
Zelensky: mobilization has already begun
Citing new intelligence data from Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR), Zelensky said more than 8,000 North Korean military personnel are currently in Russia, with preparations underway to deploy an additional 10,000.
Russian Drone Strikes Near Yahodyn Border Crossing With Poland Again
“They increased the number of people who are recruited by different methods. They plan to increase and attract foreigners,” Zelensky warned.
Currently, one in 10 Russian prisoners of war (POWs) held in Ukraine is a foreign citizen.
Ukraine’s “I Want to Live” project – which helps Russian soldiers surrender – recorded at least 55 nationals, largely from Third World countries.
For several months now, Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly warned of Moscow’s possible mobilization in autumn 2026, following the State Duma parliamentary elections, which were held for the first time since the beginning of Russia’s war.
In July, Ukraine’s military and foreign intelligence agencies estimated that the Russian General Staff had developed a plan to mobilize an additional 600,000 people – 300,000 during 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027.
Several preparatory measures have been cited as signs of possible mobilization, including tighter military-registration controls and additional penalties for ignoring electronic summonses.
The Kremlin consistently denies new mobilization.
Meanwhile, Moscow-Pyongyang military cooperation ties appear to deepen, with North Korea emerging as one of Russia’s most critical wartime partners, supplying troops, weapons and manpower in exchange for financial and technological support.
Warnings of escalation on NATO territory
Since at least the beginning of the year, several EU member states have warned that the conflict in Russia could spill beyond Ukraine’s borders, and arrive on NATO’s doorstep.
The decree comes just days after Putin, speaking on Friday, Sept. 25, denied that Moscow is preparing for war with Europe while accusing the Baltic states of violating the rights of Russian speakers and vowing that Russia would keep fighting for them.
During the same remarks, he also mocked Estonia’s security concerns as “political clowning.”
To justify its pressure on neighbors, including Ukraine before the full-scale invasion was launched, the Kremlin has long invoked alleged discrimination of Russian minorities.
Moscow has also repeatedly denied it planned to attack Ukraine. It still refers to the war in Ukraine as a “special military operation,” downplaying its significance.
This is precisely why concern keeps growing among NATO’s eastern flank.
Lithuania has recently reinforced protection of critical infrastructure, while the US confirmed a new troop rotation to the country.
Citing intelligence reports, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sept. 17 that Russia is planning hybrid drone or missile strikes on countries backing Ukraine, including Poland, which Moscow could try to pass off as accidents.
Several of the bloc’s member states have already stopped referring to the drone incursions, sabotage campaigns and frequent airspace violations as hybrid attacks and incidents, instead calling them direct attacks.
Speaking to reports during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, Zelensky again warned that Russia could target another European country with drones, missiles or even a ground operation in a bid to break Western unity and distract from its battlefield losses.
Around the same time, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who represented Russia during the UNGA as Putin did not attend, claimed that Europe might be in for a “self-fulfilling” prophecy due to its heavy spending on defense.
On Sept. 11, Dmitry Medvedev, former President and current Deputy Chairman of the Russian Security Council, threatened Lithuania would “disappear from the map of the world” in case of a conflict linked to Vilnius’ nuclear weapons ban lift.
He also claimed NATO would not invoke Article 5 to defend the country as that would mean a “global catastrophe.”
Just a week after, Lithuania announced an evacuation plan for Vilnius.
“One of the evacuation directions from the capital should be Poland,” Žygimantas Solovjovas, head of the Vilnius municipality’s Civil Protection Department told Polish Radio.

articles.title: Report: Eight US Marines wounded in Iranian strike near Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Report: Eight US Marines wounded in Iranian strike near Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN — An Iranian anti-ship cruise missile strike in the Strait of Hormuz has left at least eight US Marines wounded, exposing the mounting operational vulnerabilities of the American military presence in West Asia and puncturing Washington’s carefully curated narrative of naval dominance in the Persian Gulf.
The high-precision strike, which occurred on September 14, targeted an unauthorized maritime vessel deployed within the strategic chokepoint. According to disclosures from American officials, the impact resulted in immediate trauma among the personnel on board, including smoke inhalation and symptoms consistent with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and severe concussions. The injured troops—comprising seven enlisted service members and one officer—were attached to an expeditionary battalion landing team operating covertly aboard a non-naval, commercial-grade maritime vessel rather than a standard commissioned warship.
The incident, concealed by the United States Department of War for nearly two weeks, came to light only after the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) belatedly added the wounded Marines to its casualty rosters for Overseas Operations, without disclosing the time, location, or circumstances of the engagement. Both US Central Command (CENTCOM) and the Pentagon declined to formally address the strike, extending a pattern of information suppression and data manipulation that has characterized Washington’s public disclosures since the outbreak of hostilities in late February.
The successful missile engagement serves as a potent reminder of Iran’s comprehensive operational control over the Strait of Hormuz and adjacent littoral waters. Operating under strict rules of engagement, naval units of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) and the Army have established absolute surveillance over the waterway, through which a significant portion of global petroleum supplies must transit.
Tehran has reiterated that maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz is indivisible and sovereign. Hostile military assets and non-authorized vessels attempting illegal passage, espionage, or the enforcement of unilateral Western blockades against Iranian commerce are treated as legitimate tactical targets. Military authorities in Tehran have repeatedly cautioned foreign powers that any vessel defying Iranian navigational regulations, failing to transmit required identification, or participating in hostile maneuvers will be intercepted or neutralized without hesitation.
Despite Washington’s deployment of vast naval assets to the region—including more than 50,000 personnel, multiple carrier strike groups led by the USS George Washington and the USS George H.W. Bush, and accompanying guided-missile escorts—the Pentagon’s attempt to impose an unlawful blockade on Iranian ports has been systematically frustrated. Iranian coastal defense batteries, armed with advanced radar systems and indigenous anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, hold every foreign vessel in the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman within immediate targeting range.
US casualties and information blackout
The September 14 strike has renewed scrutiny over the Pentagon’s opaque reporting practices regarding military casualties. Since the United States and Israel jointly launched their aggressive, unprovoked war against Iran on February 28, defense analysts and regional observers have noted an unprecedented level of discrepancy and confusion in official American reports.
While DCAS records show that well over 860 US military personnel have sustained injuries since the start of the conflict, independent observers argue the true figures are substantially higher. Over the summer, the Pentagon abruptly reclassified its casualty methodologies, retroactively lowering official death counts and categorizing combat casualties under vague bureaucratic labels to soften the domestic political impact of the campaign’s escalating human toll. The delayed logging of the eight Marines—justified retroactively by US officials as a standard administrative reporting lag—reflects a broader strategy aimed at downplaying the efficacy of Iranian defensive countermeasures.
Furthermore, the deployment of combat troops aboard an undisclosed “maritime vessel” points to a growing operational shift by CENTCOM. Facing devastating losses and heightened risk to major surface combatants from Iran’s asymmetric swarming tactics, naval drones, and precision coastal batteries, the US military has increasingly resorted to utilizing auxiliary, commercial, or unmarked hulls to evade detection—a strategy that Iranian intelligence and surveillance networks continue to successfully penetrate and neutralize.
Iran’s non-negotiable terms
Iranian political leadership and top military commanders have made it explicitly clear that safe, uninterrupted transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains entirely contingent upon the United States acknowledging regional geopolitical realities and complying with Iran’s legitimate terms.
Tehran has outlined a clear path for the normalization of maritime traffic in the waterway: Washington must bring an immediate, unconditional, and permanent end to the war of aggression it initiated on February 28 alongside Israel. Iranian officials emphasize that no foreign power will be permitted to enforce a state of economic strangulation against the Iranian people while simultaneously demanding unrestricted access for its own war fleet and commercial shipping through Iran’s front yard.
More broadly, senior officials in Tehran have repeatedly affirmed that enduring peace and stability in West Asia and the Persian Gulf can never be achieved under the shadow of foreign occupation. The root cause of regional friction, Iranian authorities insist, remains the destabilizing footprint of extra-regional forces. Real security is attainable only through collective regional cooperation among Persian Gulf littoral states, predicated on the complete, comprehensive, and irreversible expulsion of all American military personnel, bases, and hardware from the region.
As long as the United States continues to pursue a reckless militaristic agenda, sponsor Israeli aggression, and trespass upon Iranian territorial jurisdiction, Tehran has pledged that its armed forces will vigorously exercise their legitimate right to self-defense, ensuring that every act of adventurism in the waters of the Persian Gulf is met with a swift, decisive, and punitive response.

articles.title: How Ukraine angered South Korea — and why it matters
articles.body:
How Ukraine angered South Korea — and why it matters
Lee Jae-myung, president of South Korea, holds a press conference at the National Palace in Mexico City, on Sept. 24, 2026. (Gerardo Vieyra/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Ukraine just angered another partner — one sitting on an arsenal of weapons that Kyiv wants.
President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Sept. 23 announcement at the U.N. General Assembly that Ukraine’s two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) were sent to South Korea was not well received in Seoul.
"It was appropriate in every aspect not to disclose, considering the many problems it may cause when disclosed, and (we) had agreed to do so," South Korean President Lee Jae Myung responded, claiming that Kyiv broke a non-disclosure agreement.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry stepped up pressure on Sept. 28 by summoning Ukraine's envoy to issue a protest.
Officials in Seoul have warned that revealing sensitive information about the POWs transfer could have security and diplomatic ramifications — and threaten the captives’ families.
As South Korea demands an apology and an explanation, the episode adds to a string of diplomatic mishaps that are marring Ukraine’s relations with international partners amid the Russian invasion.
It also comes a little over a month after Zelensky made another overture for South Korean weapons — this time, for air defenses that would protect Ukraine from Russian ballistic missiles.
Why is South Korea angry?
Kyiv announced in January 2025 that it had captured two North Korean soldiers during battles in Russia's western Kursk Oblast.
The two were among the many thousands dispatched by North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un in 2024 to bolster Russian forces in the border region, making North Korea the only country to send its serving forces to fight on Moscow’s side to date.
The POWs have reportedly expressed a desire to defect to South Korea, and the Ukrainian and South Korean leaders agreed in July to handle the matter in accordance with the captives’ wishes and humanitarian principles.
Yet Seoul has kept a tight lid on the details, previously declining to confirm whether they had arrived in South Korea, citing potential risks to their families.
The Kim regime views families of defectors as suspect, rendering them targets of harsher repression, surveillance, and forced relocation, according to media and NGO reports.
In addition to the personal safety of those involved, Lee raised concerns about potential diplomatic and security ramifications for the Korean Peninsula.
Seoul and nuclear-armed Pyongyang have been locked in a bitter rivalry since the 1950-53 Korean War, leaving the peninsula divided between two heavily armed states.
Zelensky’s announcement came mere days after North Korea launched two ballistic missiles off its eastern coast, not long after it issued threats over the joint U.S.-South Korea military drills.
Tensions in the region remain high even as U.S. President Donald Trump and his South Korean counterpart seek to de-escalate — with Lee even urging Washington to ease sanctions in exchange for the "freezing" of North Korea’s nuclear program.
The incident with Ukraine also left Lee, from the liberal Democratic Party (DPK), open to criticism from the domestic opposition.
Park Sung-hoon, a lawmaker from the conservative People Power Party (PPP), demanded that the South Korean administration explain why the transfer was kept confidential and what agreements Kyiv has breached.
"One side claims an agreement was violated, while the other maintains that no such agreement existed," Park said, as reported by South Korean media. "Instead of pointing fingers, the government must first disclose the actual details of the agreement to the public."
Crossed diplomatic wires
It remains unclear what the origin of the diplomatic confusion was, with both sides offering a different account.
"There was no such agreement (to keep the transfer a secret)," Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelensky’s advisor, said on social media on Sept. 25.
In later comments for the Kyiv Independent, Lytvyn added that it would be "strange to simply quietly send these people somewhere."
"From the whole story — and it is a long and detailed one — we only reported the fact that they had been sent to (South Korea)," Lytvyn said.
There are signals that South Korea was not completely in the dark about Zelensky’s planned announcement.
An undisclosed South Korean presidential official told the Korea Times that Kyiv has informed Seoul of its intention — but allegedly only in vague terms, without detailing how the transfer would be presented.
South Korea’s government blasted the Ukrainian denial of a non-disclosure agreement as a "falsehood… (that) seriously undermines trust between the two governments and is an action that can cause problems for friendly ties."
This is not the first time in recent months that steps or communication from Zelensky’s office has led to a diplomatic faux pas or an outright clash with Ukraine's partners or neighbors.
Earlier this month, Zelensky unveiled a new regional forum called Carpathian Eight, supposedly including eight EU and non-EU countries sitting next to the Carpathian Mountains.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar, whose country was meant to be one of the "eight," promptly corrected Zelensky, saying that Budapest is not taking part in the initiative.
A more serious rupture appeared between Ukraine and Poland in the summer, when Zelensky granted a military unit a name in honor of the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), an underground organization that fought against Soviet rule.
The step sparked a sweeping condemnation in Poland, where the UPA is seen chiefly as an organization that took part in the 1943-45 Volyn massacres — mass killings of Polish civilians in what is now western Ukraine, then under Nazi occupation.
Poland’s right-wing President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest state order, and even Ukraine-friendly Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk criticized Kyiv’s move, albeit trying to contain the fallout.
read also
Poor signal for military aid
Owing to the unending tensions with its northern neighbor, South Korea boasts one of the largest arms arsenals in the world.
The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) names South Korea the world’s ninth-largest arms exporter, accounting for 3% of global arms sales between 2021 and 2025.
For Ukraine, this makes Seoul a tempting source of materiel needed to fend off Russian aggression.
After warning in August that Russia may ask Pyongyang for tens of thousands of fresh troops, Zelensky called upon South Korea to provide Ukraine with air defense systems.
Kyiv’s reasoning is simple — North Korea’s deepening ties with Moscow help it gain valuable combat experience for its soldiers, as well as ballistic missile technology, thus threatening security of the peninsula.
The best response on Seoul’s part would be deeper cooperation with Kyiv, Zelensky argued.
South Korea’s military operates Patriot air defense systems, which are also a key line of Ukraine’s defense against Russian ballistic missiles. Patriot interceptors are in high demand worldwide as the U.S.-Iran war has depleted much of the American stockpile.
The Asian country is also rolling out its homegrown air defenses, known as Cheongung-II, which can shoot down short- and medium-range ballistic missiles.
On top of that, South Korea boasts an arsenal of K9 self-propelled 155 mm howitzers and shells, rocket launchers, tanks, and other weapons that would likely be useful on the Ukrainian battlefields.
But South Korea — yet again — turned down Zelensky’s request for arms.
The country maintains that selling weapons to an active conflict zone is against its law, and has limited its assistance to Ukraine to humanitarian and other non-lethal aid.
Nevertheless, reports from earlier in the war suggest that workarounds are possible.
The Washington Post reported in December 2023 that South Korea indirectly supplied large quantities of artillery shells to Ukraine through a behind-the-scenes agreement with the U.S.
The latest diplomatic spat and the apparent breach of trust are unlikely to bring a similar clandestine agreement any closer, however.
Tim Zadorozhnyy contributed reporting.

articles.title: What happened to the Russians Putin mobilized four years ago? Meduza follows two of them — one still at the front, the other now a deserter in Spain.
articles.body:
What happened to the Russians Putin mobilized four years ago? Meduza follows two of them — one still at the front, the other now a deserter in Spain.
The “partial mobilization” announced four years ago remains in effect: no decree has ever ended it. According to Russia’s Defense Ministry, more than 300,000 people were drafted to fight in the fall of 2022. At least 20,000 have died. Among those mobilized were Maxim, a resident of Pskov (his name and city have been changed), and Temirzhan Bayanov from Omsk. Before he was sent to the front, Maxim had little interest in the war; now he sees Ukrainians as enemies. Temirzhan tried to avoid mobilization and was caught, but eventually managed to flee abroad. Meduza publishes their accounts of the past four years.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Maxim
38 years old
Editor’s note: Maxim is taking part in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. We are withholding his real name for his safety. We understand that some of his statements may anger readers. His account, however, shows that propaganda remains effective. His testimony may also be subjective: people at the front judge what is happening chiefly by what they see in their own units and often lack a view of the broader situation. Meduza condemns Russia’s invasion and holds Russia responsible for this war.
‘It was like I’d ended up on a reality show’
Before mobilization, I had an ordinary life: family, friends, work. I worked — or still work, I don’t know how to put it, since I haven’t been fired — as a refrigeration equipment engineer. I also ran a small air-conditioning installation business. I was happy with my life and didn’t think about the war. It seemed far away, and I wasn’t very interested in it.
My son was born on September 11, 2022. There were rumors about mobilization, but I didn’t pay much attention. I didn’t believe it could affect me. What would they need me for? I wasn’t a professional soldier. If anything, I figured I’d just get in the way. We had this huge, great army, after all, and everything looked terrific on the news.
It was funny watching grown men shake with fear when they hadn’t even gotten a draft notice. One of my colleagues, for instance, quit and went either to Abkhazia or Georgia. Notices came for friends and acquaintances. Some got out of it through work exemptions; others called me and said, “Well, shall we go?” It was like you started seeing what people were really like. Guys I’d never imagined holding a rifle went without hesitation. The ones who used to beat their chests and say, “I’d rip them apart for Russia,” went quiet instead. Quite a few guys I knew decided to go, and that made me feel better, calmer.
Then October came. A lot of draft notices arrived at work because it’s a fairly large company. But the business couldn’t have kept running if every employee who got a notice had been mobilized, so the company’s chief executive went to the local authorities and sorted it out. Half my colleagues got exemptions, but only the older ones, those 50 or older. I was 34 then and, unfortunately, didn’t get one.
So on October 2, human resources called me in and handed me a draft notice, saying, “Sign it or you’ll go to jail.” I had to report to the draft office for a medical examination three days later. I’m a responsible guy, so I signed. I left work thinking, “What am I going to tell my wife?” Our baby was a month old.
I went to the draft office. They gave me a mobilization order telling me to report on October 11. I told the military commissar my son had just been born and asked for at least a deferment. He patted me on the shoulder and said, “Who is there to fight? You’ll be home in three months.” I thought, “Okay, three months it is.”
I went home. My wife was in shock. There was a huge fight, tears; she didn’t speak to me for a week. I understood, so I just kept quiet. What worried me more was money: how was my family going to eat? Nobody had ever mentioned one-time payments for mobilized men. They said we’d be paid according to rank and position, and maybe get combat pay if we were sent to the front.
A private’s pay didn’t work for me at all. I didn’t make much at my regular job — 90,000 rubles. My business brought in most of my income. Altogether, I made a little more each month than a soldier’s salary.
I had no choice. I packed the essentials in my old backpack — my company helped me buy them, by the way — hugged my wife, called a taxi, and went to the departure point.
There were other poor bastards like me there. On October 11, they loaded us onto buses and took us to a training center. I was in a daze — it was like I’d ended up on a reality show. I thought they’d take one look at us and say, “Go home, guys. We’ve got special forces and the National Guard. We can manage without you.” Right up until the bus doors closed, I couldn’t believe this was happening to me. But nobody was going to let me go.
I can’t say the training was bad. Some of the instructors were pretty good and explained things clearly. Some guys were interested; others pretended they already knew everything. My attitude was, “Well, show me your machine gun, since I’m here anyway.” They put us through our paces for two weeks. It was interesting, and I learned things.
Our unit was made up entirely of mobilized men, mostly from Veliky Novgorod and the surrounding region, as well as St. Petersburg, Moscow, and the Moscow region. They told us, “You’re mobilized. You won’t be sent into battle. You’ll be in territorial defense.” We were happy to believe them. I’d driven a truck during my compulsory military service, so I reassured myself that they definitely wouldn’t have me launching missiles.
After two weeks of training, they had us line up. A priest came and held a service. Then they put us on a train without telling us where we were going or why. Some thought we were headed to Crimea to man checkpoints. But the train sure as hell didn’t go to Crimea. It turned toward the Luhansk People’s Republic. That’s when we started to suspect we weren’t going to be in territorial defense after all, and that we weren’t being sent to man a checkpoint.
‘We learned what war really is’
At a station in the Luhansk People’s Republic, they transferred us to military Ural trucks. We rode along having fun until we reached the first city, Sievierodonetsk. There, we saw a horrifying scene: houses burning here and there, wrecked vehicles, people with their heads down. It looked, I imagine, like besieged Leningrad. Everyone in the truck went quiet. We were terrified. That’s how I ended up at the war.
We drove through Sievierodonetsk to Kreminna, where they assigned us to positions. They brought my group to a small patch of woods, gave us some provisions and a little ammunition, pointed into the trees, and said, “The enemy will come from there. Stay alert.”
We started digging and building, trying to settle in. It was hard at first. We had no supplies at all — just a pit covered with branches for the whole platoon. Thank God some of the guys were handy. We quickly made the place livable, insulated it, and put a roof on it. The hole became something like a dugout.
I can’t say the fighting in Kreminna was especially intense while I was there. Yes, the artillery fired, and we more or less got used to it. We had our first losses, and vehicles were blown up, but there were no direct clashes then. We spent six months fighting there.
The whole unit gets an assignment, and nobody cares who does what or how. Sometimes I crawl around with a machine gun. Sometimes I move into enemy-held territory ahead of an assault soldier, clear a dugout, and set up a post to watch the skies so the assault group behind me can get through safely. Other times, I carry out an assignment alongside the assault troops.
My formation is part of the Southern Group of Forces. We fought to liberate Bakhmut in the spring of 2023 and Kostiantynivka in the summer of 2026. Now we’re fighting toward Druzhkivka.
When the Wagner fighters took Bakhmut and were supposed to go rest, our formation was ordered to take over their positions immediately. The enemy figured that with the professionals gone and a bunch of mobilized rabble sent in to replace them, they should retake Bakhmut. That’s when we learned what war really was.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language daily news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
None of us really knew how to fight for real, but an order is an order. We stood our ground and held the line. It was very hard, and we suffered heavy losses, but none of us abandoned our positions.
Bakhmut was covered in swastikas and all kinds of fascist symbols. I talked to locals. I know how they [Ukrainian soldiers] terrorized and robbed their own people. And how they killed locals in Kostiantynivka whom our guys were trying to evacuate [Meduza cannot verify all of these claims]. That, to me, is fascism.
I don’t lump them all together. Of course, some of them are decent guys who were forced into the trenches. As a rule, they don’t even want to fight and surrender right away. But sometimes you run into real hard cases, especially younger guys — stubborn bastards. I remember one asshole well. We had him pinned down and told him, “Surrender, you idiot.” But he kept shooting and wounded two of our guys. When he ran out of ammunition, he threw down his rifle and yelled, “I surrender!” Seriously? You ignored us, shot at us, and now it’s “I surrender”?
‘As long as they can still get something out of you, no one will let you leave’
Then the war started changing — the first drones appeared. They made life miserable for us from the start. FPV drones are small, but one is enough to disable a vehicle or maim someone. I got my first wound — I’ve had several — from an FPV drone. It flew out of the bushes and blew up my vehicle, peppering my leg with small fragments. It was a minor wound; I didn’t even seek treatment. But I realized the war had changed. We couldn’t go racing around on top of a tank anymore, shooting at enemy infantry as if we were on safari. The drone war had begun.
Over time, drones kept evolving. Now drones of every kind have taken over the war. One cheap little Chinese gadget can easily burn up equipment worth millions [of rubles]. Charging in with a tank or an infantry fighting vehicle doesn’t work anymore — they simply won’t make it there. So most of the fighting falls to the infantry. People are expendable. If you’re lucky and they don’t spot you, you make it through. If they do spot you, you’re out of luck.
There are so many drones. They [the Ukrainian armed forces] usually have a surveillance drone hovering overhead. When it spots movement, a few FPV drones might come in and pin you down in cover, maybe in some bushes, so you can’t get out. Then the so-called “Baba Yaga” arrives — a big agricultural drone with a heavier explosive payload — and starts tearing you apart. You have very little chance against that tactic. Somehow we keep fighting.
Of course I tried to get evaluated by a military medical board and discharged, but here there are “no sick people.” My eardrum was blown out, so I can’t hear at all in that ear, and I can’t see out of one eye. But the board told me, “You can see with the other one. You can hear with the other one.” Nobody gives a fuck about your health — or about you, period. Getting discharged is almost impossible. You can go home if you’re very badly wounded, with limbs blown off, or as a “200” — dead. As long as they can still get something out of you, no one will let you leave.
Everyone’s probably thought about taking off, running away, not coming back from leave. It’s so hard to leave home. Every time you walk out the door and picture where you’re going again… I can’t explain it. I think people being led to an execution must feel the same way.
The first reason I kept going back [to the war] was the guys I serve with. If I didn’t return, they’d have problems. They might lose their leave because of me — that happens a lot. They have families too, people waiting for them. And every person counts. If I don’t come back, one of my comrades has to do his own job and mine.
Second, how could I look my wife in the eye if I hid behind her skirt every time I heard a noise in the stairwell? I’d be ashamed to face my whole family. Though I know they’d actually support me if I made that choice.
Third, where would I run? I’ve known people who spent one, two, even three years on the run. They were caught, and almost all of them are dead or missing now. So no. I’ve got myself into this mess, and I’ll see it through.
It’s a stupid war. Two Slavic peoples have been pitted against each other, and people are making money off it. Someone has no interest in ending it quickly. But then you see what those bastards [Maxim’s term for Ukrainian soldiers] are doing, how they strike civilians, their own people, how they promote fascism, and it makes you angry. I don’t understand why we’re dragging this out. All we do is threaten them and do nothing, just push ahead with infantry. Where are our much-vaunted missiles and navy? Why not flatten all of it [Ukraine] and plant corn there?
‘No brains? Storm buildings’
Everyone thinks we get paid a lot, but nobody realizes it’s peanuts once you factor in what we have to spend on army needs. If you manage to send even 100,000 rubles home, you’ve saved a hell of a lot that month.
We pay for the whole war ourselves: vehicles, gas, drone parts, food — you can’t live on standard army rations for long. The commanders [in our unit] don’t extort money, but we have a shared fund because we all understand that if we need something, nobody will give it to us, and we still have to carry out our assignments. We usually collect 20,000 rubles per person. Sometimes there are unexpected expenses: a vehicle needs repairs, or a drone pilot loses a “bird” [a drone]. Then the cost can top 50,000 rubles each.
The higher-ups don’t much care about our fund. They give you a mission, and how you carry it out is your problem. No transport? Carry the gear yourself. No “bird,” but you need to scout an area? You’ll have to go yourself. You could jump off a roof with a hang glider for all they care, as long as the job gets done. Otherwise, command can make your life miserable — by sending you on a more dangerous assignment.
Those missions mostly go to people who can’t handle their regular duties, who’ve started slacking off or screwing up. If their mistakes have serious consequences — losses of men or equipment — the response is swift: they go in ahead of the assault troops. “No brains? Storm buildings,” as we say.
If someone does his job without screwing up, nobody bothers him. Of course, he might get a riskier assignment and start yelling, “Oh no, they’ve sent me in with the assault troops.” Well, it’s a war. What do you expect?
I’ve heard that in some units you have to bribe the commander to get leave. Unfortunately, that’s not how it works with us. Our commanders find it easier just to deny you leave.
Commanders suggested I sign a contract with the Defense Ministry — they even tried to force me — but there’s no point. We’re a combat unit. Say I refuse. Where are you going to send me, to war? To the front line? I’m already here. In rear units, a lot of mobilized guys signed contracts because they didn’t want to lose their cushy posts. I haven’t signed and I won’t, for one reason: I’m sick of this army and I want to go home. If I become a contract soldier, they’ll tell me, “Where do you think you’re going? You signed the papers. Now keep serving.”
Most troops are contract soldiers now. There are hardly any mobilized men left.
Of the 35 mobilized men in my unit, only four are still alive. Some were discharged after serious wounds; most were killed.
‘We’re here, but it’s as if we’re not’
I don’t think there’ll be [another wave of] mobilization. It would be embarrassing for the state to admit that the army needs more people. And it really does. But everyone lies to everyone else, and I think that’s why we’ve gone four years without being rotated out.
I still don’t understand why the state has simply forgotten the mobilized men and is doing everything it can to hide the fact that mobilization ever happened. That men once quietly packed up and went off into the unknown — not for money or glory, but simply because they had to.
I watched the Wagner fighters go home. Other guys came to replace them, fought for six months, and then went home too, patting me on the shoulder like, “Hang in there.” Volunteers came and went home when their terms were up. But we’re treated like lepers throughout the Defense Ministry system. We have no idea what’s going to happen to us. There used to be talk about rotating us out, but that died down long ago. Nobody says anything. We’re here, but it’s as if we’re not.
I really hope all this ends soon because I’m running out of strength, mentally and physically. I don’t know where this ends. Do we fight until our legs get blown off so they’ll discharge us? Or until we’re killed?
Things were very hard for my family at first. My wife was left alone with a small child. Of course there were fights and tears. We nearly divorced. But thank God we’re both sensible people. Together, we’re waiting for the day they finally let me go or send someone to replace me. The trouble is, my son has already grown up without me. To him, Dad is just a face on a phone screen saying, “Hi, how are you?”
I don’t get leave as often as I’d like. Most of the time, I get leave because I’ve been wounded. I remember the first time was the strangest. They wouldn’t let me go for ages — I didn’t get leave until my eleventh month. Until then, we’d been living in a dugout in the woods the whole time. It was crazy. Then I came home and realized I wasn’t used to being in a city anymore. I was scared even to go to a store: it was so light and bright, with so many people. I walked around in a daze.
That’s the scariest part — how you get used to all of this [the war]. I honestly find myself thinking there never was another life. At first you wonder how you’ll sleep in a hole with none of the comforts of home. Then, after a couple of weeks, you get used to it. You get used to the shelling too. A tank can be firing nearby and I’ll sleep like the dead. But when it’s completely quiet, I can’t fall asleep, especially at home. Sometimes, when I’m on leave, I slip and say I’ll be going home soon, meaning my dugout. Now when I come home, I feel like a visitor. That’s sad.
Every day I try to stay alive, and I lose good comrades. Every time I lose a friend or fellow soldier, it leaves me depressed and stressed, especially if he dies in my arms. But the hardest part comes later, when relatives — a wife or a mother, say — call and ask you to tell them anything at all. I still get calls from families of men who died back in 2023. It’s very hard to talk to them. They’re sobbing.
So I try not to get too close to people. There are guys I serve with, and that’s enough for me. One time a new contract soldier arrived, a young guy of about 22. He’d come for the money. I looked at him and thought, “I’d give every penny I have to get out of here. And you came here without even knowing what you were getting into, because you fell for that slick picture they paint on Channel One. It’s different here.” By the time you realize you never needed that money in the first place, it might be too late.
Temirzhan Bayanov
41 years old
‘I’m not carrying that machine gun, and I don’t want to fight at all’
I’d been following the news about Ukraine since 2014. Even then, I realized the Russian authorities wouldn’t be satisfied with occupying Crimea and taking a bit of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. I knew there would be an escalation and a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It was only a matter of time.
I worked for myself. In 2016, I moved from Omsk to Kaliningrad. I wanted somewhere warmer, but not too hot, and closer to Europe. I bought an apartment there. Then I went to the Balkans. In Serbia and Croatia, I bought fruit and vegetables for shipment to Russia, working as a middleman and taking a cut.
I returned to Kaliningrad in May 2022. I’d thought mobilization was possible, but I didn’t expect it to begin so soon. I didn’t expect the Russian army to screw up on every front.
A draft notice came in mid-October. I wasn’t home. My neighbors called and said some people had come by and asked them to pass the notice on to me, but they’d refused.
I’d graduated from law school in Omsk and knew what I needed to do. I went into hiding. I canceled my registration at my Kaliningrad apartment, moved to Omsk, and registered temporarily at someone else’s address there. But they found me anyway at the end of December.
I was planning to go to Novosibirsk. Police stopped me as I entered the train station in Omsk. They asked for my documents, checked something, and found out I’d been sent a mobilization notice. They called the military police, who were supposed to take me to the draft office. I signed some paper — I think it was a mobilization order — and asked to go home to get my documents. They let me go. I was afraid of criminal prosecution, so I got the documents and went to the draft office. They processed me there and took me to Omsk’s armored-vehicle engineering institute, which was serving as an assembly point for mobilized men from across the Siberian Federal District.
There were a lot of people, and there wasn’t enough room in the barracks. So they housed some men in big tents at a military training ground near the institute. Instead of generators for light and heat, the mobilized men had a stove. They fueled it with things sent as humanitarian aid — cookies, wafers, letters from children. I was surprised but didn’t ask why. Most likely they didn’t have enough firewood or coal. Later I learned that generators were being sent as aid too, but the regimental commander was selling them off to someone.
At the assembly point, they suggested I become a machine gunner. I said, “I’m not carrying that machine gun, and I don’t want to fight at all. Is there something easier?” The political officer suggested communications, and I agreed.
The place wasn’t guarded all that heavily, so there were ways to escape. But I knew that if I ran and they caught me, I’d go to prison. I wanted to get discharged on medical grounds instead. I used to play hockey, and once I got into a fight. I haven’t been able to see well out of my left eye since. But I couldn’t get a medical discharge; they only kept promising me an examination. A lot of people who didn’t want to fight because of health problems were sent [to the combat zone] anyway.
Around mid-January 2023, they put us on a train and took us to a training ground in Baranavichy. I was sent to headquarters as a communications specialist. There I started telling [other mobilized men] what I thought: that we’d be fighting for the elite’s interests, not our own. We had one patriotic signalman there who complained to the battalion commander, and they transferred me to the medical unit.
They started training us as medics, teaching us how to give first aid. Some people said our instructors were Wagner fighters, but I didn’t ask much, and they barely talked about themselves. They just showed us, very professionally, what to do and how.
‘They sent people into the combat zone every day’
In March or April [2023], they brought us to Khartsyzk in the Donetsk region, near the border with Russia. We spent about a month there, then went to some village near Vuhledar. We lived in dugouts along the second line of defense. Two strikes landed nearby, but we were all right.
Our whole regiment was made up of mobilized men. There weren’t many true believers among them. A lot of them said, “Why did we go to this war?” But once they started getting paid, they went wild — alcohol, drugs, prostitutes.
They tried to talk us into signing contracts. Recruiters came and told us about all sorts of perks, including one-time payments. I didn’t need any of that. I knew the contract had no end date. Then again, neither did mobilization — not until the war ended.
At the beginning of August, they moved us closer to Bakhmut, to Myronivskyi. Wagner had taken Bakhmut, Klishchiivka, and Lysa Hora and was holding them. Then Wagner left, the regular Russian military took over and, to put it bluntly, fucked it up. The Ukrainians seized the initiative and took Lysa Hora.
After that, the Ukrainians started moving into Klishchiivka and bombarding it. The first [Russian] company went in and got smashed. Our company and a third were supposed to go in after them. But almost all of us — about 100–150 men, myself included — ”became 500s” and started putting our refusals in writing. Commanders from the division and armed military police officers arrived. We took up our weapons too and said, “We’re not going.” They left us alone then, but by late August they started transferring a few men at a time to Bakhmut, supposedly to headquarters, and sending them on to Klishchiivka from there. Maybe they used threats to make them go. I don’t know.
I refused [to go to Bakhmut], and they locked me up in Myronivskyi. It was in a school or some kind of building used for children’s activities. They locked me and three other men who’d refused to fight in a room, basically to make us think it over. They kept us there for four days. They fed us and took us to the bathroom; they treated us fine.
After that, they gave me an assignment: set up a medical station for the severely wounded between Bakhmut and Klishchiivka. I followed the order and set one up in a dugout. Every day, they sent 20 to 100 people into the combat zone. About 15% came back for medical care — some without an arm, some without a leg. I bandaged wounds and put in IVs. I worked nonstop. It was frightening. That’s where I saw the full horror of war.
I understand that a Russian soldier is a killer and an occupier. So I was helping occupiers. On the other hand, there’s the human side of it: was I supposed to refuse to help the guys?
‘I didn’t try to escape because I was hoping we’d be demobilized’
A week or a week and a half later, in early September [2023], our medical station was hit by a round we call a “Polka” [a round from a Polish-made 60-millimeter mortar]. I got away with a mild concussion: I felt a little sick and my ears were ringing. They took me to the medical unit, gave me IV treatment, and sent me to regimental headquarters 10 days later. There they ordered me to set up a new evacuation point to replace the medical station the Ukrainian armed forces had discovered. I got some men together and showed them where to set it up, though I was still at the old site myself. A couple of weeks later, a 120-millimeter round landed near it. Another concussion, but this time a serious one: severe headaches and a stutter that lasted a month.
They took me to a hospital in Donetsk. After treatment, I got a referral to a military medical board in Novocherkassk, the nearest city [in Russia]. I went there, started seeing doctors, and realized nobody was going to discharge me. Near the city, in the village of Persianovsky, there are military units with barracks used as headquarters. They offered to let me stay and receive wounded soldiers coming from the hospital, since I was a medic. I had a good reputation and knew how to handle the paperwork. And I didn’t want to go back “across the line.” So I stayed in Persianovsky.
In October 2024, they transferred me again, this time to a board at 7/7 Mylnikova Street in Rostov that determined soldiers’ fitness for service. But there was no transfer order — only a request — so the move was unofficial.
On the board, I helped the guys. I found loopholes so they could get treatment at civilian hospitals if the [military] hospital wouldn’t admit them. Sometimes it worked. But the higher-ups needed to keep the numbers up because there weren’t enough men at the front. Say someone had an Ilizarov frame on an arm or leg: they’d send him to finish recovering somewhere other than Russia — a hospital in Debaltseve [in the Donetsk region], for instance. And there you have no rights. You’re expendable.
My superiors didn’t like my helping the guys, and I knew they might send me “across the line.” In February 2025, some people I knew called to warn me that men from my unit were already on their way to pick me up. I found a BlaBlaCar ride to Moscow and flew from there to Kaliningrad. They put me on the federal wanted list and opened a criminal investigation. They went to my mother’s place in Omsk and threatened to send me to prison. But she didn’t know where I was.
About six months later, they caught me at the North Station in Kaliningrad. As I understand it, they tracked me through security cameras. The police took me to a station. Military police from the commandant’s office came there and took me to an assembly point for men who had refused to fight. They gave me a choice: serve at least three years in prison or go to war. I didn’t want prison, and I didn’t want to fight either. I chose prison.
Instead, the military police took me and several others on a flight to Luhansk to send us to the front. There I tried again to get discharged because of my eye. I went to an ophthalmologist and asked for a referral to Belgorod. The headquarters staff and I got along, so they let me go. From Belgorod I returned to Kaliningrad, planning to leave for Europe from there. ChatGPT suggested Tverdy Znak. I contacted them, and they planned a route. That’s how I got to Spain, where I plan to apply for asylum.
I hadn’t tried to escape earlier because I was hoping we’d be demobilized. All the mobilized men hoped for that and tried to find some way to stay in Russia instead of being in the combat zone. Some people paid bribes; I just did my job well. I didn’t go to lawyers either because I knew it was pointless. The war machine was already running, and everyone was working for it. There are no rules, no laws. The Russian army is a bunch of complete fucking assholes, and Putin and everyone at the top with him are a gang of bandits, thieves, crooks, and murderers.
But of course I wish I’d escaped even earlier. I wouldn’t be like I am now. My mental health is a mess after those two concussions. I sleep badly. I get anxious and lose my temper over nothing. I never used to be like this.

articles.title: Russia Begins Additional Mobilization, Expands North Korean Troop Presence
articles.body:
Russia has already begun additional mobilization and is preparing to extend the deployment of North Korean troops on its territory, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday, Sept. 28.
Citing new intelligence data from Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR), Zelensky said more than 8,000 North Korean military personnel are currently in Russia, with preparations underway to deploy an additional 10,000.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The longer-term plan envisions a contingent of up to 50,000, which Zelensky has been warning since at least August.
“They increased the number of people who are recruited by different methods. They plan to increase and attract foreigners,” Zelensky said according to Ukrinform.
According to the latest “I Want to Live” project – which helps Russian soldiers surrender – one in 10 Russian prisoners of war (POWs) held in Ukraine is a foreign citizen. At least 55 nationalities have been recorded.
Mounting losses and autumn mobilization plans
Ukrainian authorities have warned repeatedly that Russia might be planning a major mobilization in autumn 2026 to replenish its ranks amid high battlefield losses.
The mobilization was expected to happen after the Sept. 18-20 State Duma parliamentary elections – the first elections since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, in which there was no doubt that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia would win.
In July, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry estimated that Russia lost around 43,000 troops, while the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU) suggested in the same month that Russia recruited 1,070-1,090 troops per day on average, which fell short of the battlefield losses.
Russian Drone Strikes Near Yahodyn Border Crossing With Poland Again
Western assessments suggested that Moscow has so far delayed a formal mobilization wave by relying on volunteers and covert recruitment.
Meanwhile, the same way Russia continued downplaying the war in Ukraine – now in its fifth year – by calling it a “special military operation,” Moscow has sparked doubt in Ukrainian officials over its frequent denial of another round of mobilization.
Ukraine’s military and foreign intelligence agencies said in July that the Russian General Staff had developed a plan to mobilize an additional 600,000 people – 300,000 during 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027.
Several preparatory measures have been cited as signs of possible mobilization, including tighter military-registration controls, possible quotas for law-enforcement agencies, expanded prison recruitment, and additional penalties for ignoring electronic summonses.
According to Le Monde on Sept. 3, Putin said that “there is no scenario that would require a mobilization,” while Deputy Security Council Chair Dmitry Medvedev later supported his claim.
Deepening Russia-North Korea ties
North Korea has become one of Russia’s most critical wartime partners, supplying troops, weapons and manpower in exchange for financial and technological support.
Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) estimated that North Korea supplies between 25% and 40% of Russia’s artillery shells, while the first reported use of North Korean ballistic missiles by Russia dates back to Dec. 29, 2023, when one missile landed in a field in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region.
Late July, Zelensky said that Russia used a North Korean ballistic missile in the strike that killed a family of 10 in the Kryvyi Rih district of Dnipropetrovsk region.
Around the same time, he also said that Russia is preparing to receive 30,000 additional North Korean troops and more ballistic missile launchers.
Therefore, the latest announcement does not come as a surprise, particularly because the two countries also signed a defense pact on June 19, 2024.
North Korean troop deployments have officially been recognized by Moscow and Pyongyang in April 2025.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), Zelensky revealed that two North Korean troops were captured by Ukrainian Defense Forces in Russia’s Kursk region before being handed over to South Korea.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung criticized Zelensky’s publicly revealing of the information.

articles.title: Russia’s mass drone attacks on Ukraine have a goal—likely Ukraine’s capitulation by spring 2027, ISW says
articles.body:
Russia is likely attempting to force Ukraine to capitulate by spring 2027 through a large-scale campaign of long-range strikes, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in its 27 September report. Russian President Vladimir Putin's new theory of victory relies heavily on the mass use of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles against Ukraine, the institute assesses.
Russia keeps shifting to faster jet-powered drones that Ukraine's defenses struggle to stop, forcing it to spend scarce missiles on them. Russia's use of jet-powered drones rose eightfold from June to August, with Moscow launching around 7,700 such drones since their initial deployment, Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on 23 September. But Putin likely does not expect the campaign to last indefinitely, and he may hold off on a new mobilization until he sees whether the strikes work, ISW assesses.
Putin's modified theory of victory
Putin's modified theory of victory largely depends on Russia's ability to mass-launch cheap jet-powered Gerans that get through Ukrainian defenses often enough, the institute notes.
Even a Kremlin-linked Russian milblogger claimed on 27 September that the Russian strategy, which relies heavily on long-range strikes, is costly and cannot continue indefinitely, not least because Ukraine is hitting Russia harder too, according to the analysis.
At the same time, Putin stated on 25 September that Ukraine "must feel" Russia's "retaliatory" strikes. ISW assesses that this suggests he intends to intensify Russia's strike campaign in winter, as he has in previous winters.
If Putin is counting on Ukraine to break and capitulate this winter, he may be ignoring what the campaign will cost Russia over time, the institute notes. This strategy also counts on Ukraine's shortage of Patriot interceptors against ballistic missiles, and on the country's power grid and other vital systems giving way under months of strikes.
Until that approach runs out, Putin is unlikely to back down on his demands or agree to real ceasefire talks, ISW assesses.
Ukrainian interceptors could disrupt Russia's plan
A Kremlin-linked Russian milblogger claimed on 27 September that Russian forces launched predominantly jet-powered Geran-5 drones at Odesa, Mykolaiv, and Kyiv during the night of 26–27 September. According to the blogger, Russia's diverse arsenal of strike weapons and Ukraine's shortage of air defense assets allow Russian forces to maintain the current pace of strikes and expand the range of targets, ISW writes in its analysis.
At the same time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 September that Ukraine's interception rate for jet-powered Shahed drones currently stands at 55%. Of more than 2,730 such drones Russia had launched in September by then, Ukrainian forces had downed or suppressed more than 1,500, he added.
Ukraine is testing interceptor drone prototypes in combat conditions, Ukrainian Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov told Novyny.LIVE on 27 September. The mass deployment of interceptors capable of shooting down jet-powered Gerans could begin within several months, he added. Ukrainian companies have already successfully tested several interceptor drones capable of intercepting Russian jet-powered drones in field conditions, the institute notes.
At the same time, it remains unclear whether Ukraine will be able to scale up its interceptor program quickly enough and achieve sufficient success to disrupt the intensification of Russia's campaign during the winter, ISW notes.
Why Putin may hold off on a new mobilization
Expanding Russia's arsenal of strike weapons is cheaper than carrying out a second mobilization economically, militarily, and socially, a Kremlin-linked Russian milblogger cited by the institute claimed.
Putin may put off large-scale forced mobilization until he sees whether the strikes deliver, ISW assesses, though his officials have been laying the groundwork for it despite Kremlin denials. Still, the need to replace Russia's enormous battlefield losses could push him to order such a mobilization as early as this fall, ISW notes, as Ukrainian and other sources have repeatedly reported he is preparing to do.

articles.title: Russia beginning 'additional mobilization' of troops, North Korean recruitment, Zelensky warns
articles.body:
Russia beginning 'additional mobilization' of troops, North Korean recruitment, Zelensky warns
In his nightly video address, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Sept. 28 that Moscow is beginning further troop mobilizations following Russian parliamentary elections.
"Today, the GUR reported on the measures that Russia is planning in the future," Zelensky said. "In fact, the Russians have already begun additional mobilization - they are increasing the number of people they are recruiting using various methods."
The president said that Russia is looking to "increase the involvement of foreigners" in its armed forces. North Korea is preparing to deploy another 10,000 troops against Ukraine, in addition to the more than 8,000 military personnel currently stationed in Russia. In return for troops, Zelensky said that Russia is providing technological assistance to North Korea, and that Shahed attack drones are now being produced by Pyongyang.
"This is how evil spreads and how a threat to life in one part of the world spreads to other parts of the world," Zelensky said. "This can only be overcome together."
The president previously angered South Korea's leadership after divulging details about captured North Korean troops in his speech at the 81st U.N. General Debate.
Zelensky's warnings came as Russian state media reports that President Vladimir Putin authorized an increase in the size of Russia's armed forces on Sept. 28. Under the decree, Russia's military personnel will be set at 2,441,630, including 1,550,500 active-duty personnel. This would be an increase of 15,500 personnel.
This marks the fourth increase in the size of the Russian army since the beginning of 2025.
The additional mobilization was expected by experts following the victory of Putin's United Russia party in the nation's parliamentary elections on Sept. 21. The elections were widely viewed as rigged by election observers.
Ukrainian intelligence says Russia's General Staff is prepared to mobilize around 300,000 personnel in 2026 and 2027 each. These forces are in addition to roughly 400,000 people a year that Russia needs to recruit just to replenish its forces, a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
To help combat Moscow's troop increase, Zelensky called for further sanctions on Russia and aid from allies as Ukraine continues to be battered by widespread Russian drone and missile attacks.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia has already begun additional mobilization
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia has already begun additional mobilization
The head of state said this in his evening address, according to Ukrinform.
"Today, I also received a report from the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine on the measures Russia is planning next. In effect, the Russians have already begun additional mobilization – they are increasing the number of people they recruit through various means. They also plan to increase the recruitment of foreigners," Zelensky said.
He noted that there is new information regarding the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia. According to him, more than 8,000 North Korean military personnel are currently on Russian territory.
"In addition, preparations are underway to deploy another 10,000 troops – they are being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia," the President said.
According to Zelensky, Russia is paying North Korea for this assistance, including with technology. In exchange for such support, and with Russia's technical assistance, production of Shahed-type attack drones has been established in North Korea.
"This is how evil encroaches, and how a threat to life in one part of the world spreads to other parts. This can only be overcome together. And today, many around the world have spoken out about this Russian terror, about this cooperation between Russia and everyone who can enable even more killing. This must be countered," the President said, calling on partners to increase sanctions pressure on Russia.
As reported, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on September 28 increasing the number of personnel in the Russian Armed Forces by 15,500.
According to the decree, published on the official legal information portal and entering into force on Monday, the authorized strength of the Russian Armed Forces now stands at 2,441,630 personnel, including 1,550,500 military personnel.
Before the previous change, made in July, the authorized strength stood at 2,426,130 personnel, including 1,535,000 military personnel.
This is reportedly the fourth increase in the size of the Russian military this year and the seventh since the beginning of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes downtown Kyiv, kills one, injures 21, damages National Academy of Sciences
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes downtown Kyiv, kills one, injures 24, damages National Academy of Sciences
Key developments on Sept. 28:
- Medical center, science academy struck in downtown Kyiv as all-day Russian drone attacks continue
- Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi liberates 3 more settlements, inflicts 2,000 Russian losses, 3rd Army Corps announces
- Trump wants Zelensky to ease strikes on Russian refineries, Ukraine official says deal must go both ways
- Poland to ease rules for shooting down drones, missiles entering from Russia
- Ukrnafta installs concrete shelters at Kyiv gas stations amid Russian attacks
- Russian drone strikes near Ukraine-Poland border crossing in Volyn Oblast
Russian drones have struck central Kyiv in the middle of the day on Sept. 28, killing one and injuring 24 others, as Moscow's round-the-clock bombardment of the Ukrainian capital continues.
The Russian attack on the city center killed a woman and injured 24 other people, including three children, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Russian drones struck non-residential buildings in Kyiv's Obolonskyi, Darnytskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts, according to Klitschko.
In the city center, the Ukrainian National Academy of Sciences building was set ablaze, while Education and Sciences Minister Andrii Butenko reported that one of the ministry's buildings was also damaged.
An aide to former National Security and Defense Council Secretary Volodymyr Horbulin was killed in the strike on the National Academy of Sciences building, the academy's press service told Ukrinform. Horbulin was at work when the building was hit and sustained a minor injury, according to Suspilne.
Horbulin is one of the architects of Ukraine's missile and space programs, as well as the post-independence security doctrine, holds the highest national decoration Hero of Ukraine, and is a full knight of the Order of Prince Yaroslav the Wise.
The building is located in close proximity to important city landmarks, including the Taras Shevchenko Ukrainian National University, the capital's main opera and ballet theater, and the German embassy.
Videos posted to social media showed people clinging to the outside of windows as smoke poured from the building.
Later in the afternoon, local Telegram channels showed another strike in central Kyiv, with videos showing a medical center belonging to Ukrainian private medical provided Dobrobut in flames.
The building is just across the road from Ukraine's Constitutional Court, and only two blocks from the country's national stadium.
Zelensky confirmed the strike on the medical facility, adding that first responders were working at the scene.

Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi liberates 3 more settlements, inflicts 2,000 Russian losses, 3rd Army Corps announces
Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps have liberated three more villages in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of the ongoing Operation Vivaldi, corps commander, Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi said on Sept 28.
The villages of Ridkodub, Nove, and Katerynivka were liberated, while full Ukrainian control was restored over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka.
The latest official update from the offensive operation, which has been covered by strict operational security measures for most of its duration, marks 51 square kilometers newly liberated, bringing the total so far of territory officially retaken to 176 square kilometers.
This phase, described as the "third season" of Operation Vivaldi, inflicted over 2,000 Russian losses and saw over 250 Russian soldiers taken prisoner, according to Biletskyi.
"The idea that 'Russians don’t surrender' from movies in practice turned into entire units surrendering in full — including officers, pilots and artillerymen," the general said.
"We hope to exchange them for Ukrainian soldiers currently in captivity in the near future."
Operation Vivaldi, the corps' offensive operation around Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, was only made public on Sept. 15, although Russian pro-war Telegram channels and independent open-source intelligence (OSINT) researchers on social media had been tracking Ukrainian attacks in the area since late spring 2026.
read also
Trump wants Zelensky to ease strikes on Russian refineries, Ukraine official says deal must go both ways
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sep. 27 he once again urged his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, to scale back Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries amid a global rise in diesel prices.
Trump has previously attributed Kyiv's regular strikes on Russian oil refineries to a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices to record highs.
"This isn't really a Middle Eastern problem; this is more of a Russia problem," Trump told reporters, adding that he told Zelensky, "You gotta take it easy on the refineries."
Trump claimed Zelensky told him, "Well, we'll probably do that." The two met in New York during the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) last week, where they discussed the possibility of a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire.
A Ukrainian official told Kyiv Independent that Ukraine would agree to stop attacking Russian refineries, but only if Russia also agrees to the energy truce. According to the official, Kyiv has not agreed to anything so far.
Despite Trump's claims, there is little evidence that Ukraine's strikes are the main driver behind the global diesel price surge.
Studies show that the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has impacted diesel and gasoil supplies far more than Kyiv's strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine's KSE institute estimates that exports from the Persian Gulf fell by 152 million barrels between March and August, compared with a 68-million-barrel drop in Russian exports during the same period.
"Russian exports are down by a third, and the drop is equivalent to around 4% of the world's seaborne diesel and gasoil trade," Luke Wickenden of the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air think tank told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine has been systematically targeting Russia's oil refineries for years, and has intensified the attacks since 2025 in an effort to disrupt Moscow's wartime economy.
read also
Poland to ease rules for shooting down drones, missiles entering from Russia
Poland will change procedures for military aircraft and helicopters that engage objects entering from the direction of Russia, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Sept. 28.
Under the current peacetime procedure, Polish pilots must fly close enough to visually confirm a target in Polish airspace before firing at it.
The new procedures will replace this visual identification with so-called positive identification, meaning the radar reading alone will be enough for the pilot or the operational commander to authorize shooting down the object, Polish broadcaster RMF24 reported.
This procedure would allow Polish forces to shoot down missiles or drones entering Polish airspace from the direction of Russia faster than previously.
"Until now, we have not used such options, because they are usually reserved for a state of war or martial law," Tomczyk said. "However, given the threat, and given that Poland today faces the possibility of drones entering our territory every day, we must introduce such changes, both for the pilots and for the security of the state."
Amid rising tensions between Russia and Poland, Russia has repeatedly violated Polish airspace.
read also
Ukrnafta installs concrete shelters at Kyiv gas stations amid Russian attacks
Ukraine's state-owned oil company Ukrnafta is installing concrete shelters at 13 gas stations in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast as Russian attacks threaten fuel infrastructure in the capital region, the company said on Sept. 28.
The shelters will initially be installed at stations in densely populated areas and near major roads, available to anyone nearby, Ukrnafta chief executive Bohdan Kukura said.
"People's safety is the main priority in conditions where Russia is systematically attacking civilian facilities that cities and communities depend on in their everyday lives," Kukura said.
The company has previously used similar shelters at gas stations in front-line regions and is now expanding the measure to Kyiv and the region amid intensifying Russian attacks on the capital and surrounding areas.
Ukrnafta has already installed gabion barriers at 25 facilities in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast. Barriers at one of its Kyiv gas stations withstood a Russian strike last week, helping contain the explosion and limiting the spread of debris, Kukura added.
Ukrnafta gas stations suspend operations during higher-level air raid alerts, with staff and customers required to leave the premises and move to a safer location, the company said.
The company said it is continuing to repair damaged facilities and strengthen protection at its stations while maintaining fuel supplies.
The move comes amid a weekslong Russian aerial campaign against Kyiv that has included repeated strikes on gas stations and other civilian infrastructure.
read also
Russian drone strikes near Ukraine-Poland border crossing in Volyn Oblast
A Russian drone struck near the Yahodyn border crossing in Ukraine's Volyn Oblast, several hundred meters from the Polish border, Ukrainian and Polish officials said on Sept. 28.
Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the drone struck Ukrainian territory about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Dorohusk crossing and did not enter Polish airspace.
"Another Russian attack on western Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X. "There was no violation of Polish airspace. Our air defense systems and aircraft were ready for action."
Sources in Ukraine's State Border Guard Service told Ukrainska Pravda that the Russian attack drone struck several hundred meters from the border and did not damage the Yahodyn crossing itself.
Ukrainian monitoring channels reported Russian drones moving toward the Yahodyn border crossing during the afternoon of Sept. 28.
The strike follows a series of recent Russian attacks near the Polish border.

articles.title: Putin Wants Ukraine to Capitulate by Spring 2027 Through Intensified Strikes, ISW Says
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Putin Wants Ukraine to Capitulate by Spring 2027 Through Intensified Strikes, ISW Says
Russian leader Vladimir Putin aims to force Ukraine into capitulation by the spring of 2027 through intensified combined strike campaigns during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to a recent assessment by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
The ISW report points to statements from a prominent Kremlin-aligned military blogger who acknowledged that Russian forces are making virtually no ground advances while Ukrainian forces conduct counteroffensive operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The blogger asserted that Moscow can sustain its strikes indefinitely while progressively increasing pressure on Ukraine.
However, analysts at the ISW suggest Putin may be reconsidering his long-held theory of victory. That theory rested on the belief that the Russian military could sustain an endless offensive until achieving its goals or forcing a Ukrainian surrender.
The institute notes that Putin likely does not expect an endless air campaign, but rather intends to leverage intensified strikes to compel Ukraine to capitulate by spring 2027.
According to the analysis, this strategy relies on Ukraine’s limited ability to intercept jet-powered drones, along with potential shortages of Patriot air defense interceptors during the winter of 2026–2027.
It also assumes that Ukraine’s energy and critical infrastructure will collapse under relentless pressure in the coming months.
"Putin may not be taking into account the long-term consequences of the Russian strike campaign if he expects Ukraine to collapse and capitulate this winter. It is unlikely that Putin will compromise on his demands or enter into serious negotiations on a ceasefire until his new theory is tested," the ISW report concludes.
On September 28, 2026, a Russian attack on central Kyiv struck the Dobrobut Academy, causing a fire on the upper floors of the Dobrobut medical center in the Shevchenkivskyi district.
The strikes, which involved direct drone hits, damaged multiple facilities, including a building belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences, and killed one woman while injuring at least 19 people across the capital. Emergency crews responded to the sites to extinguish the fires and conduct search and rescue operations.
Simultaneously, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine and its European partners were actively developing a joint anti-ballistic missile system named "Freyja ," which could become operational within the next 12 months.
He emphasized the urgent need for a stronger, more independent European air shield, noting that while Ukraine was finalizing its proprietary interceptor missile, international partners possessed the advanced radar technologies and key components necessary to make the platform viable.
Zelenskyy warned that the global ballistic threat would continue to intensify due to deepening military cooperation between Russia, Iran, and North Korea, stating that Russia was placing its final bet on ballistic missile strikes against Ukrainian cities to break the population and deprive the country of its ability to defend itself.
