articles.title: Ukraine’s cheap Patriot rival now has a two-mode seeker
articles.body:
- Fire Point now lists the FP-7.x Freyja interceptor's seeker as combined infrared and radar, replacing the infrared-only seeker it described earlier.
- The company plans its first ballistic target interception with the missile around July 2027.
Ukrainian missile maker Fire Point has changed the published specifications of its FP-7.x anti-ballistic interceptor, now listing a combined infrared and radar seeker for the weapon instead of the infrared-only seeker it described earlier.
The company posted an updated specification card for the missile on X, which it calls the FP-7.x Freyja interceptor. In August, when co-founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman presented the Freyja project, Fire Point said the interceptor would use an imaging infrared seeker, which homes in on a target’s heat signature. Fire Point did not explain the change or say who supplies the radar component.
A seeker is the sensor in a missile’s nose that finds the target and steers the weapon in the final seconds of flight. Pairing infrared and radar lets a missile use both a target’s heat and its radar reflection to track it, which can help when one sensor is degraded by weather, decoys or the target’s own design.
The card lists the FP-7.x as 7.25 m (23.8 feet) long and 0.53 m (21 inches) in diameter, with a top speed of 1,500 to 2,000 m/s, or roughly 5,400 to 7,200 km/h (3,400 to 4,500 mph). It carries a fragmentation warhead, which explodes near the target and sprays it with metal pieces. The missile flies on inertial guidance, using onboard sensors to track its own position, and receives course corrections by radio from the ground while in flight.
For comparison, Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missile travels at about 2,100 m/s at the end of its powered flight, according to Fire Point’s August presentation.
The FP-7.x is the interceptor for Freyja, a pan-European project to build a cheaper ballistic missile defense system than the U.S.-made Patriot. Ukraine and nine other European countries signed a declaration launching the effort on July 13. Fire Point serves as the main system integrator and has signed agreements with 13 European defense companies, including Hensoldt, Thales, Diehl Defence, Saab, Kongsberg, Leonardo, MBDA and Safran, to supply radars, guidance, seekers and command-and-control equipment.
Fire Point is a Kyiv-based company founded in 2022 and is best known for its FP-1 long-range attack drones and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. The FP-7.x is a faster version of the company’s FP-7 ground-attack ballistic missile, and Fire Point has said the FP-7’s initial design drew on Soviet-era S-300 and S-400 interceptor designs. The company says the airframe is built from composite materials to keep costs down.
Fire Point chief executive Iryna Terekh told Janes in July that the current FP-7.x uses a blast-fragmentation warhead, which gives a low chance of destroying an incoming ballistic missile’s payload, and that the company plans to develop it into a hit-to-kill interceptor that strikes the target directly. She said the missile’s top speed is expected to rise to about 2,200 m/s as the program matures.
The company wants each interceptor to cost less than €1 million ($1.14 million), about a quarter to a sixth of the reported price of a Patriot interceptor, and aims to produce 2,000 a year. Ukraine relies heavily on Patriot to stop Russian ballistic missiles, and global supplies of those interceptors are limited.
Fire Point has said it hopes to have its first FP-7.x interceptors ready by the end of 2026 if European partners deliver the components it still needs, and plans the first interception of a ballistic target around July 2027.

articles.title: Russia hammers Ukraine's capital with major daytime drone strike
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Ukraine kill at least 7, including woman at Kyiv's National Academy of Sciences
Kyiv, Ukraine — Russia's round-the-clock bombardment of targets in Ukraine killed at least seven people and wounded more than 50 others, officials said Monday.
Moscow's forces pounded apartment buildings, offices, data centers and a building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in downtown Kyiv in a brazen daytime attack.
CBS News' Aidan Stretch was forced to take shelter again due to more incoming Russian weapons not long after he arrived Monday at the scene of the strike on the science academy.
The attacks followed a week of diplomatic efforts at the United Nations to get traction for negotiations on ending Moscow's full-scale invasion that began 4½ years ago.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov indicated Monday that the chances of making speedy headway on forging a peace settlement were bleak after recent Ukrainian attacks, including during recent parliamentary elections in Russia.
"Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months," Peskov told reporters. "That is happening right now."
On Saturday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in a fiery speech to the U.N. General Assembly that "Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the Trump administration is interested," seeking, as Moscow has done throughout the war, to portray a rift within the NATO alliance.
Russian drone attacks across eastern Ukraine
Russian drone attacks on the Kyiv region killed four people and wounded eight, officials said.
A woman was killed in a Russian strike on Kyiv's Shevchenkivskyi district on Monday afternoon, the Kyiv city military administration said. The strike hit the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, the latest cultural landmark in the capital to be damaged. Russian forces also hit a pharmaceutical company and gas stations in Kyiv.
One drone struck an office center in central Dnipro during working hours Monday, killing three people and wounding at least 12, local authorities said.
A Russian strike on a nine-story apartment building in the northeast city of Kharkiv wounded 43 people, including 11 children, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said.
Four people, including two teenage girls, were hurt when a Russian drone struck a residential area in northern Ukraine's Chernihiv region on Sunday evening, said Viacheslav Chaus, head of the regional military administration.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces struck two data centers in Kyiv, as well as gas stations in the Ukrainian capital. A distribution hub belonging to the Nova Poshta postal service was struck in the southern city of Odesa, it said.
The Russian military also hit a cargo ship in the Black Sea and another one in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk, the ministry said. The strikes aim to curb Ukraine's grain exports, though they may also create food shortages in countries that rely on Ukrainian imports.
The Russian aerial attacks regularly hit civilian areas. Moscow claims it targets only military-related sites.
Ukraine claims small gains along entrenched front lines
Battlefield positions have changed little since last year, in part because swarms of drones severely restrict troop movements, but Kyiv's forces launched a recent offensive, code-named Operation Vivaldi, on part of the 800-mile front line.
Ukraine's Third Army Corps said Monday it had recaptured another 20 square miles from the Russians, bringing the total to 68 square miles since the offensive began several months ago.
The corps said that in order to break through Russian defenses, it converted Soviet-era BTR-60 armored personnel carriers into kamikaze vehicles that blew up the strongest Russian fortifications. The operation has also used ground robots to attack Russian positions.
The claimed breakthroughs came in the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine, which the bigger Russian army has been trying in vain to conquer.
Russian officials made no immediate comment on the Ukrainian claim.
Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said Russian troops captured the villages of Novovodiane in the Donetsk region and Ulanove in the northern Sumy region.
It was not possible to independently verify the claims.
Zelenskyy said long-range strikes on Russian soil hit two defense plants in the Tula and Voronezh regions and oil facilities in the Krasnodar region, all in southern and western Russia.
Ukraine's long-range drones have repeatedly targeted Russian fuel depots and industrial plants that are a mainstay of Moscow's economy and war effort.
Ukrainian drone attacks overnight started fires at three infrastructure facilities in Russia's Krasnodar region, local emergency officials said Monday, without identifying the locations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 254 Ukrainian drones overnight.

articles.title: U.S. Embassy Issues Security Alert to Citizens in U.K. Amid Suspected Terror Plot
articles.body:
The U.S. embassy in London has issued a security alert for American citizens in the U.K. following a suspected terror plot near an RAF airbase used by the U.S. military, which led to the arrests of five men who have since been released on bail.
“U.S. citizens are encouraged to exercise caution and be mindful of personal security,” read the notice responding to the Sunday incident near RAF Fairford. “U.S.-associated facilities, gatherings, and organizations may be at heightened risk. U.S. citizens are advised to follow instructions of local authorities for their personal safety and security.”
The alert reminded Americans that the U.K. in April raised its national terrorism threat level to “severe” from “substantial,” a decision made after an antisemitic attack in London was declared a terrorist incident by police. The “severe” level, according to the Metropolitan Police, means “an attack is highly likely.”
The warning came after British police arrested five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after they were detained near RAF Fairford in southwest England, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran, in the early hours of Sunday. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base, which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) previously said could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military.
The U.K.’s Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) confirmed in a statement to TIME that the five arrestees were British nationals in their 20s who live in London. They were all released on bail Monday afternoon, local time. "They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry," according to the CTP.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme early Monday that it is too soon to speculate over the motives during a live investigation. Questioned about a potential Iran link, he said: "We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm. We know that they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies."
CTP’s deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans said she was “very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised,” but stressed more time is needed to work through the case.
Additionally, the head of CTP Laurence Taylor emphasized his officers are considering this case from "every possible angle," including the potential that this "may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."
The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. "The circulation of such fabricated speculations... will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the U.K.," it said Monday.
What we know about the arrests at RAF Fairford
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. It has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
Gloucestershire Police, the local authority responsible for the area, received a call from a concerned resident at 12:45 a.m. local time on Sunday, regarding three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the airbase.
The local resident, a farmer, told police she had found the road blocked by three white vans. “I saw a large group of hooded and masked men. When they saw me, they ran ahead of me… I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place,” she later told the BBC.
Armed officers responded to the call and five men were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act, as well as section 5 of the Terrorism Act.
Police evacuated residents from around 85 nearby households and put a cordon in place while the British Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team examined the vehicles.
While the farmer who alerted police has been hailed for their actions, Streeting has indicated they only had a “partial picture” of the matter and appeared to suggest U.K. security forces had been aware of a suspected plot involving RAF Fairford.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday claimed the suspects had been “under view for a long time.”
"Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great… and we got them,” Trump told reporters.
When asked if Trump had been correct, Streeting did not reject the assertion.
“Our security services and our police, they don’t ask for praise, but I think it was a proud moment yesterday to see the President of the United States recognize the extraordinary work that our police and our security and intelligence services do every day throughout the year and throughout the world to keep us safe,” he said. “That’s all I want to say this morning on that.”
TIME has asked the Ministry of Defense and Downing Street whether the British authorities were already investigating a potential plot.
Speaking at the Labour Party conference later Monday morning, Streeting celebrated the U.K. and U.S. alliance as “the closest of any two nations on Earth” and vowed the two countries “will always stand together against those who hate our freedom and those who wish us harm.”
British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband, meanwhile, referred to the incident near RAF Fairford as a “reminder of the threats our country faces.”
The U.K. must be prepared to “confront” all the security threats facing Europe and the world, he told conference attendees, adding that “we will act against the proxies of Iran.”
Prime Minister Andy Burnham referred to the seemingly foiled terror plot as "deeply concerning," ahead of holding a COBRA meeting (a session of the government’s emergencies committee) to discuss the incident with top advisers Monday afternoon.
Concerns over the risk Iran poses to the U.K.
The U.K. government gave authorization in March for the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The base’s role in the U.S. military’s seven-month operation against Iran may have made the site a target.
While British police and lawmakers have said it's too early to determine who was behind the suspected terror plot, the U.K. government has repeatedly issued stern warnings regarding the threat the Iranian regime poses to the U.K.
On Feb. 28, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer addressed the nation, explaining the U.K. had no involvement in the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran, but emphasizing the government’s belief that Iran cannot be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon.
“Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community,” he said. “Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil."
In March, four men were arrested on suspicion of conducting surveillance of locations and individuals linked to the Jewish community in London to assist Iran. One man was an Iranian national and the other three were British-Iranian nationals. The CTP said the arrests were “part of a long-running investigation and part of our ongoing work to disrupt malign activity where we suspect it.”
A separate investigation resulted in a man being charged in May with assisting a foreign intelligence service relating to Iran.
Earlier this month, a man and woman were arrested in London as part of National Security Act investigation. They were apprehended on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service. Again, the country to which the investigation was linked was Iran.
The IRGC was designated a threat to national security in the U.K. under new powers in July, after a series of antisemitic attacks across England., including arson offenses against Jewish ambulance services.
“These new powers will make it easier to prosecute and lock up anyone carrying out [Iran’s] dirty work here in Britain,” said Starmer at the time.

articles.title: European Solidarity initiates Verkhovna Rada Conciliation Council meeting over Russian aerial terror – Geraschenko
articles.body:
The European Solidarity faction in the Verkhovna Rada is calling for the urgent convening of a closed-door meeting of the Conciliation Council, as well as a parliamentary session, due to the continuous aerial terror campaign by the aggressor state.
"European Solidarity demands the immediate convening of a closed-door meeting of the Conciliation Council and a session of the Verkhovna Rada to address a single issue: the provision of air defense and Armed Forces equipment, and the situation regarding shelters. We need a report on the production of domestic missiles and anti-Shahed systems—things the authorities have endlessly announced. What is the status of the communications system and its protection? These are the questions... Today, we will demand that the Verkhovna Rada leadership arrange a closed-door meeting with military officials and the Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council," faction co-chair Iryna Geraschenko wrote on Facebook on Monday.
According to her, the strikes on Kyiv demonstrate just how unprotected the capital and other Ukrainian cities are against jet-powered drones, while the occupiers are "rapidly modernizing their instruments of death and ramping up production."
Geraschenko also called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to meet with the leadership of the parliamentary factions.
She later added that "this escalation is taking place against the backdrop of numerous summits and statements about 'hellish places' and millions of drones—for which billions have been allocated from the budget." "Yes, Russian occupation forces are killing Ukrainians. Yes, the world is not reacting sufficiently to these crimes (and support is dwindling further against the backdrop of government corruption scandals). But the time has come to ask the Ukrainian authorities as well: where are our cutting-edge developments—such as long-range missiles capable of striking the Russian military-industrial complex and anti-Shahed defense systems? Where are the results of your security agreements and peace summits?" Geraschenko wrote.
The MP also noted that profit margins in the defense sector within NATO countries stand at 8%, whereas in Ukraine they exceed 20%, despite the high volume of imported components. "Isn't this return on investment too high given the devastated state of the Ukrainian economy? ... Isn't it time to revise regulations and adopt NATO standards for the relationship between the state and arms manufacturers, especially considering the billions flowing from the budget into this sector?" Geraschenko wrote.
As earlier reported, a drone strike on the National Academy of Sciences building on Monday sparked a fire on the upper floors. The State Emergency Service reported one fatality and six injuries. Zelenskyy stated that three children were among the injured. Media reports identified the deceased as an assistant to Volodymyr Horbulin, the former head of the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC), while Horbulin himself was among the injured. The press service of the State Language Protection Commissioner reported that two academicians died in the Russian strike on the Academy building, and contact had been lost with several others. Ukraine's Ambassador to the UK, Valeriy Zaluzhny, confirmed that several people died in the Academy building as a result of the strike.
According to the State Emergency Service, the number of people injured in the Russian strike on the Dobrobut medical center in Holosiyivsky district has reached eight. The Kyiv police press service reported that the total number of people injured in the Russian drone attack on Kyiv has risen to 21, and one person has died.

articles.title: Putin is testing NATO on Norway’s remote Arctic islands
articles.body:
BARENTSBURG, Norway — For the best part of a century, the biggest threat to the residents of Svalbard was polar bears. Increasingly, it now comes from Russia.
Fears are growing that Moscow could use the sprawling Arctic archipelago — a part of Norway with an unusual legal status — to test NATO militarily amid growing uncertainty over the U.S. commitment to European defense.
Allies suspect Russia of probing crucial undersea cables in the waters off Svalbard and staging military-style events that test the limits of the rules governing its presence there. As Russia ramps up hybrid attacks across Europe, Oslo is racing to boost its naval and surveillance capabilities to protect its northern flank, while local authorities on Svalbard are investing in critical infrastructure — and even have an evacuation plan in place.
Advertisement
“There is more tension in the Arctic and in the north, and of course also Svalbard is a part of that,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik told POLITICO. “We know that Russia ... uses a lot of ways to try to provoke or find ways to do hybrid threats.”
Despite its status as Norwegian territory, the archipelago's main island, Spitsbergen, is home to a Russian town.
“Russian leadership is highly unpredictable and more and more risk prone,” said Kari Aga Myklebost, a Russian history professor and Svalbard expert at Norway's Arctic University. “I wouldn't close out any scenario when it comes to the Kremlin's will to confront NATO.”
High North, high tension
For decades, Svalbard symbolized the Norwegian maxim “High North, low tension,” which saw efforts to build cooperation among Arctic countries, including Russia.
Beyond its remoteness — lying over 900 kilometers from mainland Norway — and its glacial temperatures, that was down to the archipelago's unique status. Under a 1920 international treaty, countries recognized Oslo’s sovereignty over the islands and in return gained resource exploitation rights — with the Soviets buying the town of Barentsburg to mine local coal deposits soon after.
Advertisement
The treaty also forbade any nation from using Svalbard for “warlike purposes” including the construction of naval bases and fortifications, but Norway does visit the archipelago with coast guard and military vessels.
At its Cold War peak, 2,400 Soviet citizens lived on Spitsbergen, the only populated island, making up around 70% of its population.
Moscow has little incentive to upend the treaty because it could rebound against its own interests. With Russia’s northwestern Kola Peninsula — home to two-thirds of its nuclear second-strike submarines — sitting around 1,000 kilometers away, “Russia has been cautious to avoid any kind of escalation,” Myklebost said.
A Soviet-era placard in Barentsburg. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
That makes it strategic for NATO, too. “In a military conflict … this is where the Russian submarines could enter the North Atlantic and hide at greater depths and pose a threat to NATO and the U.S.,” she argued.
Yet tensions have grown following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow also began direct boat trips from Russia in 2024 and last year set up a chapter of the Russian Geographical Society, which is led by former Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu.
“We call them gray zone provocations,” Myklebost said. “It’s a very cost-efficient way of asserting Russian presence and … challenging Norway's jurisdiction.”
As a result, Norway’s intelligenceservices this year warned the Kremlin “aims to increase Russian scope for action in Svalbard.”
British, American and Norwegian forces this spring reportedly caught Russian vessels testing a secret subsea cable-cutting weapon off Svalbard’s coast.
Although Barentsburg’s coal reserves are dwindling, Moscow is not abandoning the town. Moscow provided state-owned Trust Arktikugol, which administers Barentsburg, with about 1.89 billion rubles (€20 million) in federal subsidies in 2025, according to its accounts.
Russia’s ambassador to Norway, Nikolay Korchunov, told POLITICO he wanted to see a “transformation of the economic activities” from coal to services in Barentsburg, and said Arktikugol was investing in maintaining the town.
Advertisement
Cranes and scaffolding adorn many of Barentsburg’s Soviet-era buildings, which lie scattered across a jagged hill facing the imposing snow-specked Vøringen glacier — a sign of Russia’s continued interest.
But “we are not questioning any sovereignty of Norway,” Korchunov insisted. “We stress the necessity and importance of fulfilling all the Svalbard Treaty,” he said, accusing Oslo of contributing to a “negative trend towards NATO militarization of entire Baltic-Arctic region.”
On thin ice
Vice Adm. Rune Andersen, the chief of the Norwegian Joint Headquarters, said his priority was “striking that balance between deterrence but maintaining stability” on Svalbard, and remaining “calm and collected” on hybrid threats.
Svalbard Deputy Governor Katharina Rise. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
But given the “risks” of escalation, the military is investing to reinforce its surveillance capabilities, he said, including launching three new maritime mapping satellites next year — alongside “a renewal of the navy and coast guard … to have a continuous presence” nearby.
NATO countries “are more often up in our waters,” said Sandvik, the minister. Defending Svalbard is also a part of NATO’s planning process, he said.
Advertisement
Locally, the strategy is to keep a lid on tensions. Svalbard’s Deputy Governor Katharina Rise said her office meets with Russia’s local consulate four times a year. “We have good and constructive dialogue,” she said. “It's our responsibility to secure the stability and … low tension here.”
Terje Aunevik, the mayor of Longyearbyen, the main Norwegian town on Spitsbergen, said authorities had plans in place to rapidly evacuate the settlement if tensions flare.
With just two subsea internet cables, one airport, one water reservoir and one diesel-run power plant in Longyearbyen that depends on imports, Aunevik said “major investments” are underway, including the construction of two new water reservoirs by around 2029. “We are quite vulnerable in that perspective,” he said.
Out in the cold
Up close, Barentsburg doesn’t look particularly threatening. Few locals venture outside the several dozen crumbling buildings. A plume of smoke escapes the aging coal plant and a lonely hammer-and-sickle Soviet flag flaps in the wind. Barentsburg feels like an abandoned relic of a bygone era.
Some of the recent hybrid activity is also down to a local push for attention from Moscow, said Arild Moe, a research professor and Russia expert at the Fridtjof Nansen Institute think tank. “They’re playing on nationalist strengths … to get priorities and to get finance.”
But Putin’s unpredictability and Trump's repeated wavering on NATO remain wild cards.
Anxiety is also palpable on Spitsbergen. In Barentsburg, “we don’t speak about [political] topics,” said a waitress from St. Petersburg who asked that her name not be used, while acknowledging locals fear a potential NATO-Russia war. “Of course this worries us,” she said.
“There is of course this constant chatter about if the Russian government wants to push a NATO member and Svalbard is the place where they would do it,” said Jonatan Svensson, an expedition guide who has lived in Longyearbyen for five years.
Jonatan Svenssson. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
To assuage those fears, NATO should consider air patrols over Svalbard, shift defensive air assets to the north of mainland Norway and hold joint exercises nearby, the two NATO diplomats said, provided Oslo agreed and the measures complied with the Svalbard Treaty.
However, so far NATO has no public plans to boost its naval or air presence around the islands. But some worry the alliance's current posture won't be enough to deter Moscow.
In theory, it would be “really easy” for Russia to occupy Svalbard, said Ståle Ulriksen, a lecturer at the Royal Norwegian Naval Academy, if it flew in special forces from northern Russia and seized the airport. However, he argued such a scenario is unlikely.
Yet Moscow wouldn’t need to launch a full occupation. According to Myklebost, the analyst, Russia could stage an emergency affecting its local citizens and send in crisis management forces, a move that may not clearly trigger NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause.
“A worst-case scenario is a situation where Moscow sees an opportunity to test NATO cohesion,” she said. “Maybe Norway's shouting for help from allies, and then you have Donald Trump saying: ‘No — we are not risking our good deals with Russia over this tiny island.’”

articles.title: US Pacific Commander Paparo discusses defense of Taiwan
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the US Pacific Command, will appear on the cover of Time magazine's Oct. 12 issue, with the magazine publishing an interview Thursday in which he discussed how a potential Chinese invasion of Taiwan could be deterred.
“I'm almost quoting Sun Tzu when I say winning without fighting is the acme of skill,” Paparo told Time, referring to the ancient Chinese military strategist and author of “The Art of War.” “Mission success for me is not to fight and win a war; it's to provide a deterrent capability so that we never go to war in the first place,” he said, per Time.
Paparo's command oversees approximately 400,000 military and civilian personnel across the Indo-Pacific region. The US Pacific Fleet consists of about 200 ships, including five carrier strike groups, and nearly 1,100 aircraft.
Paparo's primary mission is to deter aggression in the Indo-Pacific, with preventing a conflict over Taiwan a central concern. Time described his task as persuading Chinese leader Xi Jinping that the costs of using force against Taiwan would be prohibitively high.
“Twenty-five years ago the People's Liberation Army Navy was about 37 warships, and today it's 12 times that,” Paparo told Time. “Just in the last 18 months they've delivered two cruisers, eight destroyers, eight frigates, an aircraft carrier, 11 submarines, four amphibious ships, and four long-range combat logistics ships.”
He said he was particularly concerned about China's advances in space and missile capabilities and the rapid expansion of its nuclear arsenal. “They're moving toward world reach,” Paparo said.
Paparo described his current task as a delicate balancing act: ensuring China understands US military capabilities and the risks of conflict while protecting sensitive information that could let an adversary develop countermeasures.
He described the US approach as “deterrence by denial,” which seeks to convince an adversary that an attack cannot achieve its objectives. “We are not seeking the overthrow of the Communist Party,” Paparo said. “It's just that you should know that where America's direct vital interests are involved, there's a high probability of denying your aggression,” per Time.
Paparo has also proposed creating what he calls a “hellscape” in the Taiwan Strait if deterrence fails. The concept involves using large numbers of relatively inexpensive, mass-produced precision drones alongside conventional high-tech missile firepower to prevent or significantly delay a Chinese amphibious assault on Taiwan.
The strategy draws partly on lessons from Russia's war against Ukraine, where extensive use of drones has transformed the battlefield. Paparo first publicly described the hellscape concept in 2024, saying the US could deploy large numbers of uncrewed underwater, surface, and aerial systems around Taiwan to buy time for the US, Taiwan, and other partners to respond to an attack.
“We need not gain air or maritime superiority of a space; we need only deny its use to aggressors,” Paparo told Time.
Time noted that direct US military intervention in a Taiwan Strait conflict would not be automatic. Paparo's role is to build and maintain a military capability capable of countering China, while decisions about whether and how the US would intervene in a conflict would ultimately rest with the US president.
The Taiwan Relations Act provides the legal framework for US relations with Taiwan and calls for the United States to make available defense articles and services necessary for Taiwan to maintain sufficient self-defense capability. It does not require the United States to automatically defend Taiwan militarily in the event of an attack.
The potential costs of a conflict were highlighted by a 2023 war game conducted by the Center for Strategic and International Studies. In most of the scenarios examined, US, Taiwanese, and Japanese forces prevented China from successfully occupying Taiwan, but the losses were severe.
The CSIS study found that the US could lose two aircraft carriers and 10 to 20 large surface combatants in most scenarios, along with approximately 3,200 US military personnel. The US and allied forces would also lose dozens of ships, hundreds of aircraft, and thousands of personnel.
The war game was conducted before the recent war in Iran and therefore did not incorporate subsequent changes in US weapons inventories and munitions availability.
Paparo nevertheless expressed confidence in the US military's ability to prevail in a conflict. “I am confident in our ability to prevail,” he told Time. “What I am working toward is the margin by which we do, and that margin expresses itself in lives, capability, money, and time. I want to drive that bill down to zero.”

articles.title: U.S. Navy’s newest destroyer arrives in Alaska
articles.body:
- The future USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), a Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, arrived in Whittier, Alaska, on Sept. 27, 2026.
- The U.S. Navy will commission the ship there on Oct. 3, the first Navy commissioning in Alaska since 2013.
The U.S. Navy’s newest destroyer, the future USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), arrived in Whittier, Alaska, on Sept. 27, less than a week before it is due to be formally commissioned there in a ceremony the state has not hosted in more than a decade.
The Flight III Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer will be commissioned Oct. 3, 2026, in the small port town on Prince William Sound, the U.S. Navy said. Commissioning is the ceremony at which a ship officially joins the fleet and the crew takes charge of it. The last Navy ship commissioned in Alaska was the amphibious transport dock USS Anchorage (LPD 23), in Anchorage on May 4, 2013.
The ship is named for Ted Stevens, a decorated World War II Army Air Corps pilot who went on to represent Alaska in the U.S. Senate for four decades and became a leading voice on defense spending. It is the first Navy warship to carry his name. Alaska’s congressional delegation and state officials pushed to hold the ceremony in the state, and then-Secretary of the Navy John Phelan approved Whittier as the location in March.
After the ceremony, the destroyer will not stay in Alaska. Its homeport is Naval Station Norfolk, Virginia, where it arrived in May after delivery trials.
Ted Stevens was built by Huntington Ingalls Industries’ Ingalls Shipbuilding division in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and delivered to the U.S. Navy in December 2025. It is one of the Flight III ships, the latest version of the Arleigh Burke design, which has been in production since the 1980s and makes up the backbone of the U.S. Navy’s surface fleet.
The main change in Flight III is the AN/SPY-6(V)1 air and missile defense radar, which can detect and track aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles at longer range than the SPY-1 radar on earlier Arleigh Burke destroyers. The ship also carries the Aegis Baseline 10 combat system and has more electrical power and cooling capacity to run its newer sensors and weapons. The destroyer displaces about 9,700 tons and can carry out air defense, ballistic missile defense, anti-submarine and surface warfare missions.
Holding the ceremony in Alaska ties the ship to the U.S. Navy’s growing presence in the far north. The Navy said it maintains a persistent operational presence in Alaska, including high-latitude maritime security operations, and the state sits along the northern Pacific and Arctic sea lanes that link North America with Asia.
Ted Stevens is part of a steady stream of new Flight III destroyers entering the fleet from Ingalls and from General Dynamics’ Bath Iron Works in Maine. The U.S. Navy has not said where the ship will make its first deployment or when it will join a carrier strike group.
The commissioning ceremony is scheduled for Oct. 3 in Whittier.

articles.title: Ukraine is asking for a truce. So why is it preparing for a bigger war?
articles.body:
Ukraine is asking for a truce. So why is it preparing for a bigger war?
Washington is pushing for an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine. Kiev supports the initiative, and Moscow has also responded favorably. Another round of shuttle diplomacy has taken place: US President Donald Trump met with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, and a special representative of Russian President Vladimir Putin traveled to the US for talks with his American counterparts. Work is underway to revive the trilateral negotiation format involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US.
Judging by these and other news reports, one might get the impression that things are moving toward a diplomatic breakthrough and a truce between Russia and Ukraine. However, this impression is deceptive: A closer analysis reveals that the positions of the parties have not changed over the past year. On the contrary, Ukraine’s worsening situation has hardened its resolve to fight to the bitter end.
Up the down staircase
In spring 2025, Ukraine, with the backing of its European allies, launched a major campaign for a ceasefire. The expectation was that Trump would force Putin to accept the terms imposed by Europe and Ukraine, freezing the hostilities along the line of contact without any preconditions.
A truce would have cemented Ukraine’s defeat in the conflict. However, Russia’s primary objective would not have been achieved: The anti-Russian regime in Kiev would remain in place, and Ukraine would retain its role as a Western foothold against Russia. A temporary truce would allow Ukraine to recover and prepare for revenge in the future. A year ago, despite major issues, Ukraine still functioned: The remnants of the civilian economy operated, and despite considerable disruptions, steel and agricultural production (two of the country’s main export sectors) continued.
Without Western financial aid, Ukraine would have already faced a financial catastrophe; however, it continued to exist. Despite occasional disruptions, major industrial facilities remained operational, as did the small and medium-sized businesses that supported them – suppliers, transport companies, various outsourced services, construction and repair crews, and so on. Cafes, restaurants, the telecommunications sector, and small businesses stayed open. Ukraine’s robust logistics sector remained active. The government collected taxes from all these businesses.
However, in spring 2026, Ukraine decided to force Russia to conclude a truce by starting a ‘war on cities’ – large-scale strikes on the Russian rear. It first targeted oil refining and export facilities, and then the civilian sector, including the warehouses of companies such as Wildberries and Ozon.
The worst possible moment
Escalation only makes sense when ‘escalation dominance’ can be maintained. Otherwise, the outcome will be detrimental to the party that started the escalation. That is exactly what happened: In response to Ukraine’s attacks, Russia launched a broad offensive against Ukraine’s civilian sector.
From the start of the conflict, Ukraine has not concealed the fact that it uses civilian logistics infrastructure to transport military cargo. Launchers for long-range drones targeting Russia have often been hidden under the guise of civilian trucks.
Ukrainian strikes on Black Sea oil and grain exports gave Russia a pretext to respond in kind and effectively block Ukraine’s shipping in the Black Sea. As with strikes on warehouses, Russia maintained the upper hand in the escalation. There are several reasons for this: Russia’s increased firepower, the depletion of Ukrainian air defenses, and more broadly, Ukraine’s smaller size, its lack of strategic geographic depth, and fewer targets within the country. While the ‘war on cities’ affected Russia as well, Ukrainian strikes did not cause the same amount of damage.
All this prompted Zelensky to propose a truce. What he actually proposed was returning to the way things were before this year’s escalation, and pretending like it never happened. But does he really want a truce? It may look that way. After all, the Ukrainian economy – and consequently the Ukrainian state itself – is beginning to disintegrate; Ukraine’s key exports – its only source of revenue aside from foreign aid – have been effectively destroyed. For the first time in history, steel production in Ukraine has come to a complete halt; restarting it would take months if not years. By all accounts, the country is facing the most difficult winter yet. If this is not grounds for making political concessions, then what is?
The only available option
Zelensky’s calls for a truce are accompanied by opposing statements. One moment, he demands a “winter package” of weapons from Trump; the next, he declares that the war will not end until Crimea is “liberated.” Domestically, he is intensifying the crackdown on the Russian language and the Orthodox Church, even though this only heightens tensions within Ukrainian society. Clearly, given these parameters, Russia will never agree to a ceasefire. So is it all just schizophrenia or a calculated move?
I’d say it’s the latter. It’s true that if we consider Zelensky as the leader of Ukraine, then his actions are insane and amount to suicide. However, if one views him as the military proxy of Europe’s anti-Russia coalition, then everything falls into place.
For Zelensky and his regime, Ukraine is not their own land; it is a resource and an instrument for war against Russia. To save Ukraine, Zelensky must accept Russia’s terms. Yet Ukraine’s masters cannot accept Russia’s terms, as that would mean a crushing defeat for them.Consequently, the war must go on. If the destruction of rear-area logistics and energy infrastructure does not affect the ability of the Ukrainian army to hold the front line, then logistics and energy don’t matter. Of course, left without electricity, heat, and jobs, Ukraine’s civilian population will endure great suffering – but Zelensky doesn’t care about that.
Taking this logic into account, even an energy truce is bad for Ukraine, as a moratorium on mutual strikes would deprive Kiev – or rather, its masters – of the only effective leverage over Moscow.Of course, this is a one-way street. In an earlier article, we analyzed how the Ukrainian state is becoming detached from its own society. Today, I’d like to point out that in its current form, the Kiev regime has no other options: On one side of the scale lies the fate of Ukraine, and on the other, the interests of its masters. Zelensky has no real choice. In the interests of its masters, Ukraine must sacrifice itself and inflict the greatest possible damage on Russia, or if possible, even defeat it.
As long as there remains hope for Russia’s defeat, nothing else matters. Ukraine wants to either freeze the conflict along the line of contact and prepare to take revenge later, or fight to the bitter end. Russia understands this very well; that is why it has once again rejected any idea of a partial truce – this was recently expressed by Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov at the UN, and then by Putin. Even though this year, Russia was seriously affected by Ukrainian strikes, Moscow is only open to ending the conflict on its own terms.
***
What comes next? Both sides are actively preparing for the winter campaign, and it appears that, for the first time since the start of the conflict, long-range air strikes (the war on cities) will become the primary theater of operations. Moscow is confident that the Ukrainian army cannot inflict strategic damage on Russia; consequently, its only option is to maintain escalation dominance by responding to the Ukrainian strikes with even more powerful attacks. Under these circumstances, there can be no talk of either an energy truce or freezing the conflict along the line of contact.

articles.title: Chinese shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles appear in Russian service
articles.body:
- Russian state TV footage shows a Russian air defense unit with unmarked shoulder-fired missiles resembling China's QW-18A and QW-19, Militarnyi reported.
- The launchers were filmed with a mobile fire group of the 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region.
Russian air defense troops appear to be using Chinese-designed shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles, according to an analysis by Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi of footage aired on Russian state television.
The launchers were shown during an exercise by a mobile fire group of Russia’s 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region, in a segment broadcast by the state channel Rossiya 1 and shared on X by the account TheDeadDistrict. Mobile fire groups are small teams, often riding in pickup trucks, that Russia uses to hunt Ukrainian drones with machine guns and short-range missiles.
The soldiers in the report called the weapon “Iva.” But the launcher does not match any man-portable air defense system, or MANPADS, known to be in Russian service, Militarnyi reported Sept. 28. Russia’s own shoulder-fired missiles in current use include the Igla-S and the newer Verba.
Militarnyi said the launcher most closely resembles Iran’s Misagh-3 and China’s QW-18A and QW-19. Neither the launchers nor the missiles shown on camera carried any visible markings, which the outlet said could point to an effort to hide where they came from.
A closer look at the footage favors a Chinese origin, according to Militarnyi. The Russian launchers have an extra fitting on the front section that does not appear in available photos of the Iranian Misagh-3. The outlet did not rule out that it could be a newer Iranian version, but said no photos of Misagh launchers with that feature have been published. Militarnyi said it could not determine whether the system is a QW-18 or a QW-19. China’s state-owned CASIC showed the QW-19 at the DSA 2024 defense exhibition in Kuala Lumpur.
The weapons may have reached Russia through Iran, Militarnyi said. Tehran buys Chinese arms, including shoulder-fired missiles, and in July 2026 reports emerged that an Iranian deal with China covers up to 400 MANPADS, including the QW-12 and FN-16, at an estimated cost of $60 million to $70 million. Iran’s Misagh family is itself derived from China’s QW series, and Pakistan builds a similar missile under the name Anza-2.
Militarnyi said Russia’s use of foreign-made shoulder-fired missiles may indicate that its own industry cannot produce enough to meet the military’s needs. Mobile fire groups have become a main line of defense against the long-range drones Ukraine sends against Russian refineries, airfields and weapons plants, which increases demand for short-range missiles.
Ukraine has previously said it confirmed Chinese supplies of gunpowder and artillery systems to Russia, and Ukrainian intelligence services believe military cooperation between the two countries includes producing Chinese-designed weapons inside Russia. China has repeatedly said it does not supply lethal weapons to either side in the war.

articles.title: Software Deals Move Mobility Fleet Toward Common Operating Picture with Real-Time Data
articles.body:
A recent $21 million contract award to three software companies could give the Air Force’s airlift and tanker units real-time software updates in degraded environments, including aircraft fuel, logistics, and other mobility fleet data.
The Defense Innovation Unit and Air Mobility Command announced Sept. 15 they have awarded deals to Defense Unicorns, Stator Integration Labs, and Air Space Intelligence, each providing different tools to move the prototype software to production and deployment across AMC platforms.
The effort is under the umbrella of AMC’s Open Mission Engine program. Dubbed OMEN, the program is aimed at giving aircrews and mobility commanders better real-time information in denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited environments.
An AMC spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the program seeks to have “present, current, and usable” aircrew mission software without a reach back or needing to connect to ground networks or cloud infrastructure to obtain the necessary update.
The program is still in its prototype phase, the AMC spokesperson wrote in an email, so they could not share initial and full operational capability timelines.
Officials have described OMEN as creating a “common operating picture” for mobility forces that have long lacked sophisticated connectivity. Using edge computing, the system will be able to track fuel, deliver software, and fuse data to create that common operating picture across the fleet, which will then load into aircraft cockpits and tablets.
Defense Unicorns CEO and cofounder Robert Slaughter told Air & Space Forces Magazine that’s “what makes OMEN special.”
“There’s a lot of different AMC assets, and they all need a common operating picture,” Slaughter said.
A former Air Force major, Slaughter explained that OMEN will fuse data across multiple inputs to give each user a clear understanding of what’s happening where and when.
“I think the biggest thing is: how do you do that on your worst day, and I think that’s key. How do you get software delivery done?” Slaughter said. “Accelerate the speed of software delivery on the nation’s worst day, and that’s what OMEN’s ultimately all about.”
The goal, Slaughter said, is to get on-demand software updates in the users’ hands.
“That’s measured in hours, not months or weeks,” he said. “That is a gnarly problem.”
Mark Lepczyk, Air Space Intelligence’s vice president of defense, says that as things stand, mobility crews wind up “pulling numbers from separate systems and reconciling them while the situation keeps evolving,”
“Under DIU’s OMEN program we’re reading crucial data like fuel state directly from the aircraft, fusing it on the same screen with the threats, the weather, and mission details, and offering optimal course of action recommendations, so the crew can now make accurate decisions at machine speed,” Lepczyk wrote in an email.
ASI’s application, which creates the common operating picture via data fusion tech provided by Stator Integration Labs, runs on a tablet that aircrews currently carry, Lepczyk said.
“The aircraft and the command center are working from identical information. It connects to existing Air Force systems, shared data services, and beyond-line-of-sight connectivity. A traditional operating picture tells you what is happening right now,” Lepczyk wrote. “Ours projects forward, so if weather suddenly shifts 300 miles ahead, the crew immediately understands all impacts and options to mitigate.”
The OMEN software assesses the “ripple effect” of any disruption to fuel, timing, or mission objectives and then gives the user “executable options” to replan quickly, Lepczyk wrote.
“We configured our solution assuming that any network can fail. Data can be cached locally, and the applications intuitively cue the crew if any information is degraded or stale,” he wrote.
Finding the Tools
DIU sought a software solution with both open-source protocols and a purpose-built capability stack tailored to OMEN’s needs, , unit spokesperson Caroline Thompson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
The unit works with military organizations such as Air Mobility Command and industry vendors as a kind of middleman, finding the right prototype solutions to military problems.
OMEN fleet software is part of a larger DIU effort to get quickly updatable and upgradable software in action across all Pentagon entities, Thompson wrote.
“The OMEN project exemplifies DIU’s strategy to bridge this gap,” she wrote. “By establishing an air-gapped-native fleet management layer, OMEN is building a repeatable framework to push software updates and AI capabilities directly onto operational aircraft. This project provides Air Mobility Command with a scalable blueprint to keep tactical edge software current and mission-ready.”
Delayed software impacts are felt across the fleet.
“This agility is key because software is only useful if it can be accessed and updated in the environments where it is required, in this case, on aircraft in austere locations or at 35,000 feet in the air,” Thompson wrote.
Defense Unicorns’ Unified Defense Stack-Fleet software is what Airmen will be using through the OMEN program. Components of UDS software have been used to upgrade F-22s, F-16s, and C-17s.
Slaughter, who deployed as an Airman with AMC assets, is keenly aware of what delayed software updates can do to a fleet. Often, software updates on legacy platforms can be a depot-maintenance level task.
“The jet not only goes through a maintenance period on the flight line, but the jet has to fly somewhere and be grounded completely out of the fight,” Slaughter said. “That is huge. I mean, I have vulnerabilities in the system, and I need to patch these. Imagine the entire fleet saying, ‘Hey, all of you have to go to depot-level maintenance, and it’s going to take several days or a week per plane’…You literally couldn’t fight and win wars with that posture.”
While Defense Unicorns’ UDS software will run on large platforms such as airlift assets and tankers, the software can be trimmed down for fighters and even drones, Slaughter said.
And while contractors are running the software updates in the prototype phase for OMEN, Airmen will be taking the reins once it reaches the production phase, Slaughter said.

articles.title: Ukraine's defense industry gets a second chance
articles.body:
Ukraine's defense industry gets a second chance
A soldier from the "Taifun" unmanned aerial vehicle unit holds a new model of the "Marsianin" attack drone in Kharkiv region, Ukraine, on April 7, 2026. (Nikoletta Stoyanova/Getty Images)
Daria Yaniieva
President of Defense Builder
In 1991, Ukraine inherited the second-largest defense industrial complex of the Soviet Union.
It was so big that almost a third of the Soviet space industry sat on Ukrainian soil, and the system employed millions of people. Pivdenmash, a rocket and space technology juggernaut, built the most powerful intercontinental missiles on the planet. Antonov, a world-famous brand, produced the world's largest aircraft. The city of Kharkiv designed tanks, and Mykolaiv launched aircraft-carrying cruisers.
Nevertheless, within a single generation, much of that capacity had disappeared, and by 2014, the former Soviet Union's second-largest defense producer left volunteers shouldering much of the burden of supplying the army defending Ukraine against Russia's first invasion.
Today, Ukraine is building its defense industry for the second time, and in a way opposite to the Soviet one: from the bottom up, with private money, in open competition, under the harshest quality control in the world — the front line.
According to research by Defense Builder and KSE Institute, a sector dominated by state enterprises before the full-scale invasion now counts more than 1,000 companies, and private business accounts for up to 90% of activity in drone production.
In 2025, the industry produced $13.1 billion worth of output, 31% more than a year earlier. And that is only the funded share of what is possible. The state puts the sector's capacity at tens of billions of dollars. The most important thing, though, lies beyond the figures.
The longer I work inside the sector, the more convinced I am that the real question is what kind of Ukraine this industry will make in 10 years. History here is merciless and useful at once.
In the first scenario, the defense industry becomes the root system of the state, from which much else grows.
In the United States, Silicon Valley grew out of military radar labs and Pentagon contracts; the internet and GPS came from defense programs.
In Israel, the defense sector spawned an entire technology economy. Signals intelligence Unit 8200 still serves as the talent incubator of the cybersecurity industry, and defense exports have set records five years running, reaching $19.2 billion in 2025.
South Korea built its defense industry into a broader industrial push and today ranks among the 10 largest arms exporters in the world, with an ambition to become the fourth.
The second scenario we know from our own history.
By Western estimates, the Soviet defense complex absorbed 15–20% of the entire economy. It lived behind the fences of closed cities and made civilian goods by quota. Soviet television sets came partly from defense plants, cameras from military optics, and Pivdenmash itself produced tractors between missiles.
As soon as the market opened, all of it disappeared almost overnight. Not a single civilian line of the defense complex became an industry able to live without an order from above.
There are a handful of structural road forks a country passes early on its way that separate these two scenarios, and Ukraine has to choose and pass them right now
Fork one is a closed loop or spillover. Do military technology, people, and engineering culture flow into the civilian economy, or stay inside a closed circuit?
The American and Israeli models won on spillover. Ukrainian technologies in autonomy, communications, robotics, and electronic warfare have obvious civilian continuations in agriculture, space, and so on.
But spillover has to be built. It is created by intellectual property rules, education, and dual-use mechanisms. If we seal the sector "for security reasons", we will repeat the Soviet trajectory in miniature.
Fork two is autarky or openness. Japan built technologically superb weapons exclusively for itself, having banned its own arms exports, and within a few decades, its defense industry withered: microscopic production runs, sky-high unit costs, manufacturers closing their defense divisions one after another.
Korea and Turkiye went the opposite way, building their industries with exports in mind from the start, and it was foreign markets that gave them the scale that keeps an industry fit.
Ukraine has spent more than four years in forced autarky and is leaving it right now.
In early July, the government formalized a transparent mechanism of controlled exports, open only to those who simultaneously meet the needs of the Ukrainian army. Our own military gets its weapons first.
We jumped off the Japanese trajectory at the last moment. But a mechanism that exists on paper still has to be made to work. Permission only opens the door, and exports are far from the only mechanism. International revenue also comes through joint ventures, where the partner gains access to technology proven at the front and the Ukrainian company gains scale, capital, and a presence in foreign markets.
The interest is obvious: by the KSE Institute's preliminary estimate, 156 international defense partnerships have already been launched.
At the same time, a quarter of them have already stalled. Openness becomes an industry only together with service, standards, financial instruments, and constant work on the markets, and all of that still has to be built.
Fork three is competition or consolidation from above. In 1993, the Pentagon gathered the heads of the largest defense contractors for a dinner that went down in history as the "Last Supper" and told them: there are too many of you, merge.
Within a few years, the industry had shrunk to five giants. About 22 years later, William Perry, the man who hosted that dinner, publicly admitted that the experiment had turned out badly.
Competition disappeared, prices rose, and innovation slowed so much that outsiders like SpaceX and Anduril had to break the system open.
Ukraine is being built on the opposite principle — open procurement cycles in which hundreds of manufacturers compete for contracts.
That competition is what gives Ukrainian defense tech its speed of innovation. From the outside, the number of players can look like chaos begging to be tidied up. But the market will consolidate the sector on its own in time.
Fork four is doing everything or specializing. In 1987, Israel canceled its own Lavi fighter program.
The decision passed the cabinet by a single vote, the country took it as a national humiliation, and Israelis still argue about its price.
But the main thing happened. Israel admitted it could not carry everything, and the engineers and budgets it freed went into sectors where it became first in the world — avionics, air defense, unmanned systems, electronics.
We, too, will have to say honestly what we are not going to build.
Our advantages are obvious: unmanned systems in every domain, electronic warfare, and, most valuable of all, combat data.
That is where the margin lies that cannot be copied, because years of front-line experience cannot be copied. This advantage has already been paid for, at a price no other country will want to repeat. And it is exactly what international partners are ready to pay for, with contracts, joint ventures, and investment.
Finally, fork five is an island or an archipelago. Korea's defense industry rose from the start together with shipbuilding, the car industry, and electronics within a single industrial policy, and each sector reinforced the others.
A defense industry either pulls a component base, machine tools, engineering education, and capital markets along with it, or remains an island in someone else's ocean.
These forks will have to be passed through institutions — rules of the game, education, standards, capital instruments, validation, and analytics infrastructure.
History rarely gives a second chance, and Ukrainians have managed to become the exception, which we should duly use this time.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: Kyiv Science Academy hit, 10 dead as Russian jet-drones strike across Ukraine
articles.body:
Kyiv Science Academy hit, 10 dead as Russian jet-drones strike across Ukraine
KYIV, Sept 28 - At least two people were killed when a drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv on Monday, as Russia pounded the heart of the Ukrainian capital with some of the most persistent drone strikes since the start of the war.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said nine people had been killed and more than 80 injured in Russian drone strikes throughout the country.
Two people were killed in the assault on the Academy of Sciences building in the heart of the capital. Emergency services said later in the evening that one of the dead had been recovered from under rubble.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 24 people had been injured in several attacks on the capital, six of whom were being treated in hospital.
Sirens echoed through the streets as smoke billowed into the sky and air raids sounded late into the day.
In recent weeks, Russia has begun hitting Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with faster, high-flying jet drones.
In his nightly video address, Zelenskiy said Ukraine was still having difficulty countering faster, high-flying Russian jet-powered drones -- 90 of 120 drones fired on Ukraine were jet propelled, rather than propeller-driven, and the interception rate was 57%.
"New interceptors are being actively tested," he said. "Some combat groups are using them, but, of course, some details still need to be refined to achieve enough effectiveness and scale. Wea re speeding up the developers."
Oficials had noted attacks on other targets, including a pharmaceutical company, petrol stations and a medical facility in Kyiv. In other cities and regions, civilian facilities, businesses and communications infrastructure were targeted.
Zelenskiy also detailed a report from Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) which he said showed that Russia had launched a new wave of mobilisation for its military.
"They are increasing the number of people they recruit through various methods," he said. "It is important that the governments of countries from which Russia recruits people for its army take action against this."
He said 8,000 North Korean troops, first brought to Russia in 2024 to counter a Ukrainian incursion into Kursk region, remained in the country and a further 10,000 were Being trained.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed as "utter nonsense" any notion that Moscow is ordering a new mobilisation.
ATTACK ON BUSINESS CENTRE IN DNIPRO
In the southeastern city of Dnipro, the Russian drone attack on the business centre killed three, officials said.
In particular, Russia has been widening its attacks on economic targets beyond warehouses, port facilities and energy infrastructure, in recent days hitting data centres and telecoms facilities.
Another person was killed in a logistics office in Synelnykove, southeast of Dnipro, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Emergency services said an attack on infrastructure in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured 32 people.
In Kyiv, flames leaped from the opened interior of the historic Academy building, and rubble was strewn across the courtyard, partially burying one car. Firefighters doused the building in water and searched for people in the wreckage, while two survivors of the blast clambered from upper storey windows, onto ladders raised by emergency services.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of cynicism for targeting a scientific institution during the working day.
"Russia is deliberately expanding the boundaries of what it believes the world will tolerate. Every attack left without a strong response only encourages the next one," he said, calling on Ukraine's allies to provide it with more air defences.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said 19 people had been injured in the daytime attack on the business centre in Dnipro.
Hanzha said the centre was surrounded by residential buildings, a park, a library and offices in the city centre: "Hundreds of people are here in the middle of the working day."
Ukraine has also increased attacks on Russia, targeting oil refineries as well as online retailers to try to undermine revenues and support for Moscow's war effort.
Zelenskiy said on Monday that it had struck Russian oil facilities in the Krasnodar region and two defence plants.
Both sides have denied deliberately targeting civilians. REUTERS

articles.title: Government to Prioritize Defense and Social Spending Amid Tight Public Finances, Koretskyi Says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s government, led by Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, announced that it adopted a decision setting the priority order for state expenditures, as public finances remain under strain during the country’s fifth year of war.
In a statement published on Monday, Sept. 28, Koretskyi said that the government will fund mainly defense, pensions, social payments and public-sector salaries, while postponing nonessential spending.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Under these conditions, we continue to adopt strict anti-crisis measures to ensure the most important priorities – defense needs and the welfare of our people,” Koretskyi said.
According to him, part of the planned international funding had not yet arrived due to unfulfilled obligations to international partners.
The task is clear, Zelensky says
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the meeting with the prime minister and Ukraine’s broader diplomatic team shortly after.
The government, Presidential Office, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs were presented with a clear task; to cover Ukraine’s existing defense financing needs.
“Everything that can be done together with partners, using partner funds – primarily concerning defense procurement – must be completed 100% by the end of the year,” Zelensky said, adding that full financing must be ensured.
He said he expects decisive backing from lawmakers, adding that if the government meets its commitments by Oct. 15 to secure the financing Ukraine requires, parliament must adhere to an equally clear schedule.
Vučić Resigns: What This Could Mean For Ukraine
New construction and repairs remain on hold
The announcement comes as Ukraine already increased the teachers’ salaries by another 20% starting Sept. 1, following a 30% increase earlier this year.
For teachers holding in-person classes in frontline areas, an additional payment of Hr. 2,600 ($58) will be retained.
Koretskyi said on Aug. 31 that Ukraine will move away from the Unified Tariff Scale – the standardized public-sector pay system – and adopt a model that sets base salaries according to an educator’s position and a benchmark tied to Ukraine’s average wage.
The government has also extended a program covering full tuition cost for veterans’ children in the 2026-27 academic year on Sept. 8.
However, spending deemed less urgent will now be put on hold, including new construction, reconstruction and major repairs that are not critically important, as well as public amenities such as parks, squares, fountains and street repaving.ž
Koretskyi said the projects will be carried out later, but resources must now go to critical areas.
“It is time, finally, to stop spending money on non-priority items,” he said, urging local self-government bodies to set similar priorities in their own budgets and to cut spending that is not currently essential.
$27B defense shortfall
During an interview for the “Yedini Novyny” national telethon on Sunday, Sept. 27, Koretskyi reiterated that Ukraine’s defense budget is short of $27 billion.
The government plans to cover about $7 billion of that gap through a strict austerity regime, including expenditure optimization and reallocation of funds.
Military pay and support for soldiers’ families will be provided in full.
The remaining $20 billion is expected to come from international partners and Western mechanisms. “These funds are critically needed to equip the Defense Forces with drones, missiles, vehicles and other means,” Koretskyi said.
Despite the budget deficit, pensions and salaries for doctors and teachers must be paid on time and in full, he said, adding that Ukraine has no other option.
Koretskyi pledged that by Oct. 15 the government will adopt all decisions required to receive the international aid partners have promised.
He again called on lawmakers, regardless of political affiliation, to pass the bills on which external financing directly depends, saying each step should be judged by whether it “leads to the survival of the state, the nation, our sovereignty.”
Interceptor production
As one of the key tasks, Koretskyi named scaling up production of interceptors to counter Russian jet-powered drones, which Moscow increasingly relies on to strike Ukraine nationwide.
The jets are significantly harder to intercept due to their high speed, which can reach up to 400-600 kilometers per hour (230-270 miles per hour).
To speed up production, the government is easing conditions for manufacturers, cutting red tape and expanding financial support through credit instruments, Koretskyi said.
As of Sept. 19, Ukrainian forces have developed and successfully deployed a new interceptor drone to destroy Russian jet-powered Shahed strike drones.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump said he made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to domestically produce Patriot interceptors it urgently needs to protect itself against Russian ballistic missiles.
On Sept. 8, Ukraine announced that it was signing contracts with partners for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles ahead of the winter.
Around the same time, Germany announced it would urgently transfer the PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from its own Bundeswehr (German military) stocks.
Bracing for winter
Ukraine is entering its fifth winter significantly better prepared than last year.
According to Koretskyi, the country has built more generating capacity, provided more critical facilities with backup power, increased protection for critical infrastructure and expanded its reserves of equipment, spare parts, repair crews and machinery.
However, Russia has also adapted, Koretskyi said, pointing to jet-powered Shaheds and the stockpiling of ballistic missiles and rockets.
“It will not be easy, but we have no option other than to hold out,” he concluded.
Beyond the Patriots, Koretskyi urged European partners to deploy their emergency services, including equipment and personnel.
On Sept. 27, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced almost €710 million ($809 million) in EU support for displaced people and crisis relief worldwide, €52 million ($59 million) of which will be allocated to Ukraine ahead of winter.
Less than 10 days earlier, European Pravda reported that an EU-proposed €100 billion ($115 billion) funding package for Ukraine remains largely undisputed in negotiations on the bloc’s upcoming seven-year budget, spanning from 2027-34.
Around the same time, the EU disbursed €3.3 billion (roughly $3.7 billion) to Ukraine for the procurement of missiles and drones.
Separately, the EU approved a €6.1 billion ($7 billion) defense package for Ukraine on Sept. 11, allowing Kyiv to purchase the PAC-3 Patriot interceptors.
According to von der Leyen, the EU has already mobilised nearly €15 billion (approximately $17 billion) to Ukraine in 2026 alone.
