articles.title: The enemy’s narrative of control over the Strait of Hormuz has been challenged
articles.body:
The enemy’s narrative of control over the Strait of Hormuz has been challenged
Khorasan, in an analysis of Iran’s repeated seizure of enemy equipment in the Strait of Hormuz, wrote: The IRGC Navy has announced the capture of a second advanced uncrewed surface vessel (USV) belonging to the terrorist US military.
Twenty days earlier, the IRGC had also captured the first advanced enemy drone vessel. At the time, the Pentagon claimed that the incident had been caused by a technical malfunction. The repeated seizure of enemy assets in the Strait of Hormuz has not only challenged Trump’s claims regarding control of the strait, but has also highlighted the capabilities and strength of Iranian forces in intelligence gathering and electronic warfare. Another significant point is the connection between these captures and the targeting of several vessels described as violating regulations in the Strait of Hormuz. Taken together, these developments once again demonstrate the falsity of Trump’s claims about control of the Strait of Hormuz. In other words, besides facing setbacks in surface engagements, it is also experiencing defeat in subsurface warfare.
Jam-e-Jam: Washington’s scenario is a war of attrition until the elections, then a return to hard confrontation
Jam-e-Jam examined recent developments and the US approach toward Iran. According to the paper, a comprehensive assessment of recent statements by Trump, the activities of the State Department under Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and the positions adopted by American security institutions suggests that the United States is skillfully managing a dual-track strategy. On the one hand, it is keeping the door to diplomacy open as a means of containing Iran, while on the other, it is intensifying military preparations behind the scenes. Washington has no desire to reach a meaningful compromise or ease sanctions before the results of the November midterm elections become clear. Trump’s current strategy is based on a suspended war of attrition. Within this framework, Washington is allegedly exploiting the willingness of Iranian diplomats to engage in talks and return to the so-called Islamabad understanding. By doing so, it seeks to keep Tehran’s strategic initiatives, such as closing the Strait of Hormuz or responding reciprocally to aviation-related sanctions, in a state of suspension. The United States is reportedly preparing itself to move, after passing the electoral hurdle, toward a phase of direct confrontation or the imposition of surrender-like conditions, relying on the accumulation of threats it has already established.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: The story is not over yet
Donya-e-Eqtesad published an article regarding Trump’s rejection of Tehran’s seven-day proposal. According to the paper, Iran presented a seven-day proposal in New York. Under this plan, if a series of measures sought by Tehran were implemented, the process of reopening the Strait of Hormuz would begin, while negotiations aimed at ending the conflict and resuming nuclear talks would proceed simultaneously. Trump, however, rejected the proposal. Nevertheless, the US president’s reaction should not necessarily be interpreted as an end to diplomatic communications. A key point emphasized in Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s remarks is the distinction between Trump’s public comments and Washington’s official response conveyed through negotiation channels. Araghchi does not suggest that Trump’s statements are unimportant. Rather, he indicates that Tehran is still waiting for the United States’ final position to be communicated through intermediaries. This distinction is significant because last week’s negotiations also largely followed this mechanism. Messages were exchanged between the two sides through Qatar, Pakistan, and other regional channels. There was even a meeting between Araghchi and Steve Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
Arman-e-Emrooz: The countdown to determining the future of Iran-US negotiations
Arman-e-Emrooz, in an article, referred to intensive efforts by mediators to arrange another meeting between Iranian and American officials. These efforts are particularly focused on New York, where mediating parties hope to use the remaining time available to draft a ceasefire proposal and create conditions for the restoration of free maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. The primary objective is that, after achieving initial progress on this sensitive issue, the main negotiations can continue at a faster pace in locations such as Doha, Muscat, or a European city and ultimately reach a conclusion. This approach reflects the mediators’ desire to create a new diplomatic environment and reduce existing tensions, which have had far-reaching effects on both the region and the wider international community over recent months. The dual-track policy of remaining open to dialogue while firmly adhering to core principles continues to be the cornerstone of Iran’s current foreign policy. Relying on its diplomatic efforts across multiple dimensions and on the implicit support of many countries for its principled position, Iran considers itself prepared to enter negotiations founded on mutual respect and the protection of its legitimate rights.

articles.title: Taiwan builds drone industry park to shed Chinese supply chain
articles.body:
- Taiwan broke ground on an aerospace and drone industrial park in Chiayi on Sept. 28 and opened a new NCSIST drone research campus.
- The park aims to build a drone supply chain free of Chinese components and is planned to host about 100 companies.
Taiwan broke ground Monday on an aerospace and drone industrial park in the southern county of Chiayi, where the island’s main military research institute wants to build a drone supply chain free of Chinese parts.
President Lai Ching-te led the Sept. 28 ceremony, which also opened a new Minxiong campus for the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, known as NCSIST, the state-run institute that develops most of Taiwan’s homegrown missiles and military drones. The institute did not say at the ceremony how much the new park will cost, how many companies have signed up or when it will open.
The Minxiong campus took three years to build. It includes a research building, hangars, laboratories and facilities for integration testing, and NCSIST says engineers there can work on every stage of a drone’s development, from designing the airframe to building the propulsion and flight-control systems and testing the finished aircraft. The campus also uses digital twin technology, which creates a virtual copy of an aircraft that can be tested in simulation before a real one flies, along with artificial intelligence and virtual reality tools.
The industrial park going up next door is meant to bring manufacturers, government agencies, universities and researchers together around shared computing power and digital engineering tools. NCSIST describes the goal as a “non-red supply chain,” the term Taiwan uses for components and systems that do not come from China. Chiayi County Magistrate Weng Chang-liang said in August that the park is planned to hold about 100 companies.
Taiwan’s push for its own drones picked up after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, where both sides used drones on a massive scale and Ukraine initially relied heavily on Chinese-made DJI models. Concerns that Chinese drones and parts could be tracked or cut off have pushed Taiwan to require that drones bought by public agencies come from non-Chinese supply chains.
The new park builds on the Asia UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center, which opened in August 2022 in Puzi City, also in Chiayi County, on a site that had sat empty for years. The center now hosts more than 50 drone companies and institutions, and Weng said in August that demand has outgrown its space, with another 40 to 50 firms waiting to move in.
The industry has grown quickly. Taiwan’s drone output reached NT$12.9 billion ($407 million) in 2025, about 2.5 times the 2024 figure, and exports totaled NT$2.95 billion ($93 million), according to the Ministry of Economic Affairs. In October 2025, the Executive Yuan, Taiwan’s cabinet, launched a six-year, NT$44.2 billion ($1.39 billion) program to develop the uncrewed vehicle industry, with a goal of pushing annual drone output above NT$40 billion ($1.26 billion) by 2030.
That spending has faced political resistance. In July, the Ministry of Economic Affairs warned that cuts proposed by the opposition Kuomintang, which controls the legislature, would hurt the industry. Weng has also pressed lawmakers to approve more than NT$40 billion ($1.26 billion) in drone-related procurement funding.
Taiwan’s drone strategy relies on three tiers: buying larger military drones from the United States, having NCSIST develop mid-size military drones, and buying small dual-use drones from Taiwan’s private sector. The Minxiong site is designed to link the institute’s military work with those private companies.

articles.title: Houthis say 26 Saudi airstrikes hit Yemen as gov't forces step up operations
articles.body:
SANAA, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Sunday that Saudi warplanes had carried out 26 airstrikes across five Yemeni provinces over the past 24 hours, while government forces said they had conducted hundreds of attacks against Houthi military targets in the past three days.
In a statement posted on social media platform X, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said that Saudi F-15 fighter jets operating from Khamis Mushait Air Base carried out the strikes on Taiz, Al-Jawf, Marib, Dhamar and Saada provinces.
Sarea said the strikes caused casualties but gave no detailed toll, adding that they brought the number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the current escalation began to 1,085, a figure that could not be independently verified.
Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces said Sunday that they had carried out 756 attacks against Houthi positions, personnel, and military capabilities across several areas of Yemen over the previous 72 hours.
Majid al-Nuzaili, a spokesperson for the government forces, said in a statement on X that the operations destroyed or disabled military vehicles, missile launchers, weapons depots and other equipment.
Al-Nuzaili said that 2,316 Houthi fighters were killed or wounded in the operations.
There was no immediate response from the Houthis to the government forces' claims.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthi group has intensified across southwestern Yemen recently after the group seized the strategic port city of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait earlier this month.
Yemen's conflict began in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: The Netherlands to provide EUR 10 mln to modernize two training centers in Ukraine
articles.body:
The Netherlands will provide EUR 10 million to modernize two training centers in Ukraine, Dutch Defense Minister Dilan Yeşilgöz-Zegerius said during a meeting of European Union defense ministers in Brussels.
According to the Dutch Ministry of Defense, the main topics on the agenda in the Belgian capital were hybrid attacks by Russia, military support for Ukraine, and the situation in the Middle East. The Netherlands, along with other European countries, is investing in the modernization of training centers. The goal is to facilitate the training and preparation of Ukrainian soldiers in a high-tech environment.
"Good training can literally save your life on the battlefield. Dutch soldiers have contributed, among other things, to the EU Military Assistance Mission to Ukraine (EUMAM). Thanks to this mission, nearly 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers have already undergone training. We have also provided specialized training for mechanics and tank crews. At the same time, we also have a lot to learn from the Ukrainians. After all, they have the most experience on the modern battlefield. In this way, we are building a unique partnership that makes us both stronger," Yeşilgöz-Zegerius said.
With winter approaching, the minister emphasized the importance of European allies continuing to provide comprehensive support to Ukraine. She stated that the Netherlands remains unwavering in its support for Ukraine.
"Drones, air defense, and F-16 support remain key priorities in this regard. Our support also directly contributes to our own security. The Ukrainians have shown that if we support them, they are capable of successfully repelling Russian attacks," Yeşilgöz-Zegerius said.
In February 2026, Denmark said it would finance the modernization of the infrastructure at the Ukrainian Armed Forces training center. Denmark is investing approximately EUR 33 million in training infrastructure, living and sanitary conditions, equipment, and drones for training.
An implementation partner – the international charitable foundation "Come Back Alive" – has been engaged in the project; the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense had previously signed a Memorandum of Cooperation with this organization.

articles.title: Germany Concludes “Red Storm Charlie” Civil-Military Defense Exercise in Hamburg
articles.body:

Germany Concludes “Red Storm Charlie” Civil-Military Defense Exercise in Hamburg
Germany’s Bundeswehr, civil emergency services, and private corporations have concluded “Red Storm Charlie,” a major three-day joint defense exercise in Hamburg involving 1,700 participants, German public broadcaster NDR reported on September 26.
The large-scale exercise simulated a range of hybrid threat scenarios across the city and port infrastructure, including neutralizing explosive-laden drones over port terminals, responding to chemical spills, and managing train sabotage, according to NDR.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The defensive exercise took place against the backdrop of an escalating Russian hybrid war in Germany, which has evolved from online disinformation to physical sabotage and state-sponsored terrorism, UNITED24 Media reported.
With German authorities recording over 165 acts of sabotage in 2026 alongside confirmed explosive drone strikes targeting critical sites like Leipzig/Halle Airport, civil and military leaders view joint training drills as vital for confronting Moscow’s expanding threat landscape.
On the night of September 24, a military convoy of 70 vehicles moved through the city under police escort.
September 26 drills, on the other hand, focused on mass-casualty evacuation using underground field emergency rooms and helicopter airlifts to the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf.
Civil-military cooperation expanded significantly for this third iteration of the annual drill, with civilian partners increasing from 12 last year to 60, NDR noted.
Participating entities included local emergency responders, regional authorities, and major industrial firms such as Airbus and port operator HHLA, according to NDR.
Retail conglomerate Schwarz Group—owner of the Lidl and Kaufland chains—was among the key new corporate partners. The group supplied secure, resilient IT network infrastructure to maintain communications for both civil security forces and military personnel.
Bundeswehr Commander Kurt Leonards commended the growing coordination between military and civilian actors, telling NDR that public perception of the armed forces is shifting positively as Germany adapts to a heightened threat environment.
“We receive many friendly gestures at the intersection. Soldiers are invited for coffee. We’ve never experienced anything like this before,” he said.
Hamburg Deputy Mayor Katharina Fegebank similarly emphasized that the exercise was not intended to spread fear. It was about preparing together for a changed situation.
However, the maneuvers triggered widespread local protests, with police reporting that up to 5,000 demonstrators gathered in central Hamburg under slogans opposing urban militarization, NDR reported.
Demonstrators from anti-NATO groups, climate activists, and roughly 1,900 students protesting against conscription attempted to block rail tracks in the port and disrupt military convoy routes across the Elbe bridges.
Following the completion of “Red Storm Alpha” in 2024 and “Red Storm Bravo” in 2025, military spokespersons confirmed to NDR that planning for a fourth iteration, “Red Storm Delta,” is already underway as Germany continues strengthening its civil defense framework.
European capitals are also debating an “Emergency Security Protocol” and a “counter-hybrid playbook” to coordinate joint responses to Russia’s escalating campaign of hybrid warfare, sabotage, and cyberattacks across Europe.
Designed to flank NATO's Article 4 consultation process, the proposed European Commission framework aims to allow swift, unified countermeasures against non-military aggression, despite skepticism from some diplomats over potential bureaucratic overlap.

articles.title: What is known about arrests at US airbase in Britain
articles.body:
Suspected plot to attack UK's Fairford airbase, used by US: What do we know?
LONDON, Sept 28 - British police said on Monday they were investigating whether individuals acting for a foreign state were involved in an apparent plot to attack an airbase used by the United States, but said five men they had arrested would be released on bail.
Below is what is known so far about the incident at RAF Fairford:
WHAT HAPPENED AT FAIRFORD?
Police were called to the airbase, 90 miles (145 km) west of London, early on Sunday morning by a local farmer who said she had seen three large white vans parked near the base and a group of "hooded and masked men" running into a field nearby.
Armed officers from the local force, Gloucestershire Police, responded and arrested five men in the Whelford area, about a mile from the base.
The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of offences under the explosives act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act after counter-terrorism police took over the investigation.
About 85 households were evacuated from properties near where the three vehicles were found and a 400-metre cordon was put in place around them.
WHY WERE THE MEN RELEASED?
The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said on Monday afternoon the men were being released after "extensive interviews and inquiries" and that they remained under investigation.
"They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others," he said.
He later said the incident was being considered from all angles, including whether offences had been committed "by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
WHAT DO WE KNOW ABOUT THE MEN WHO WERE ARRESTED?
The five men detained were all British nationals aged between 23 and 25 who lived in London, police said.
An image on social media purported to show some of the suspects, seated shirtless with hands behind their backs, after their arrest. Reuters was unable to independently locate and verify the source of the photograph.
WHY WOULD FAIRFORD BE A TARGET?
Fairford, which opened in 1944 and was used by allied troops for the D-Day invasion of Normandy, has this year been used by US forces for strikes on Iran.
It is one of the US Air Force's only European airfields suitable for heavy bombers, and played a key role in both the first Gulf War in 1991 and the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect Fairford after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow US bombers to fly from the base. The Guards said any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.
Over the last six weeks there has been increased surveillance in the area after a specific threat from the Iranians, according to a local councillor.
WHAT HAVE PEOPLE SAID SO FAR ABOUT THE INCIDENT?
The farmer, who has not been named, told British media she saw eight to 10 men running from the vans with their faces covered and that they got within about 100 metres of the perimeter fence of the airbase.
"I just can't process how that base was on such high alert, and that the men were even there," she said, adding that a blockade had focused only on the main entrance.
"I'm really glad they ran away."
British Defence Minister Wes Streeting told BBC TV he was grateful to the witness but that she only had a "partial picture" of what had happened after she said she was "staggered" it had been left to a member of the public to report them despite the heightened threat.
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday the group had been under investigation as part of a long-running investigation. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding that the suspects intended "big damage" to the base.
Iran's embassy in London said in a statement on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" about Tehran's possible involvement in the incident. REUTERS

articles.title: URCS assists two victims during cleanup following Russia's airstrike on Kyiv
articles.body:
The Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) was working at the sites where the aftermath of the Russian drone attack in downtown Kyiv was being addressed.

articles.title: Taiwan’s history of trapping invaders
articles.body:
The Chinese idiom “closing the door to beat the dog” (關門打狗) has evolved from a rural proverb into a polarizing strategic metaphor.
While modern Taiwanese leaders reject its derogatory language, the core tactic — luring an enemy into enclosed terrain, sealing escape routes, and launching an inescapable attack — is deeply woven into Taiwan’s legacy of resistance. Over centuries, local forces have repeatedly used geography and strategic choke points to resist stronger adversaries.
The folk and architectural blueprint
In traditional courtyards, catching an aggressive dog required shutting the main gate first to trap the animal. This found a physical manifestation in traditional East Asian military architecture through the wengcheng (甕城), or barbican system — walled enclosures built outside fortress gates that trapped invading forces inside a lethal bottleneck.
In 1948, Mao Zedong formalized a similar concept into military doctrine during the Liaoshen Campaign to isolate Nationalist forces at the Jinzhou railway junction.
However, long before and after Mao’s maneuvers, people in Taiwan adapted similar forms of entrapment as tools for survival.
Pre-Japanese and colonial resistance
Because Taiwan’s geography consists of dense forests, mountains, and narrow valleys, local resistance forces often relied on terrain to neutralize better-equipped conventional armies.
During the Lin Shuang-wen Rebellion of 1787–1788, Lin’s rebel forces faced Qing troops sent to suppress the uprising. According to accounts of the campaign, rebel forces exploited difficult terrain and fortified mountain positions while resisting Qing advances.
During the 1895 Japanese invasion, local Hakka and Hoklo volunteer militias under Wu Tang-hsing used the rugged terrain around Baguashan in Changhua while confronting advancing Japanese forces.
The battle became one of the largest engagements of the 1895 resistance and a defining example of how terrain shaped the fighting.
The 1930 Wushe Rebellion offers another example. Seediq Indigenous fighters under Mona Rudao used the difficult Mahebo terrain, including narrow mountain routes and suspension bridges, against Japanese forces.
Resistance fighters cut at least one important suspension bridge during the uprising to slow the Japanese advance. Japanese forces eventually responded with overwhelming military force, including aircraft.
The authoritarian reversal and postwar defense
During the 228 Incident and subsequent White Terror era, the logic of containment was tragically turned inward by the KMT authoritarian state.
Security forces used martial law, arrests, searches, port controls, and large-scale security operations to suppress dissidents, intellectuals, activists, and others deemed threats to the regime.
Two years later, however, geographic containment played a very different role during the Battle of Guningtou on Kinmen.
Former Japanese Imperial Army General Nemoto Hiroshi secretly traveled to assist KMT forces fighting the Chinese Communists and later advised Taiwan’s military leadership.
During the battle, PLA troops landed on Kinmen but became separated from reinforcements as Taiwan’s defenders used armor, artillery, air power, and coastal defenses to destroy or disable landing craft and isolate the invading force.
After approximately three days of fighting, the PLA landing force was defeated. The battle halted the immediate Communist advance on Kinmen and became one of the defining military encounters of the early cross-strait confrontation.
Modern cross-strait rhetoric
Today, Beijing has revived the idiom during military encirclement exercises around Taiwan.
Chinese state media and military commentators have used “closing the door to beat the dog” to describe scenarios in which PLA forces seek to cut Taiwan off from external support while preventing forces on Taiwan from escaping.
Taiwanese commentators have also used the phrase in a different context to warn taishang against moving manufacturing operations to China, where attractive incentives can later give way to regulatory pressure or restrictions once businesses are deeply invested.
The phrase remains potent enough to trigger domestic controversy.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, then-Taipei Mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) used “closing the door to beat the dog” to describe his containment strategy during a major outbreak associated with Huannan Market.
Ko said the strategy involved concentrating screening and vaccination efforts among the highly mobile market population. His choice of language nevertheless drew criticism for its blunt and dehumanizing imagery.
The modern Western reversal
More recently, the metaphor has been applied to US-China diplomacy.
A Liberty Times analysis published after the September Trump-Xi summit argued that Western democracies — particularly the United States under President Donald Trump — had effectively turned the concept back against Beijing.
Unlike the psychological deception of the classic “Empty Fort Stratagem” (空城計), which relies on bluffing an opponent, the article portrayed the summit as a structural form of containment.
Washington offered Xi Jinping a lavish welcome and the prestige of a White House state visit while continuing to maintain extensive economic and technological restrictions on China.
The underlying argument is that ceremonial engagement does not necessarily translate into strategic concession. Washington can offer diplomatic theater while continuing to constrain Beijing in areas such as advanced technology, trade, and artificial intelligence.
Taiwanese agency
Crucially, this geopolitical contest is not merely a game played between superpowers. Taiwan possesses its own historical and contemporary agency and continues to use asymmetric defense and strategic maneuvering to secure its sovereignty.
Today, one source of Taiwan’s leverage lies in its “silicon shield” — its central position in advanced semiconductor manufacturing through TSMC.
In a conflict, this technological dominance would not function as an absolute barrier. Instead, Taiwan’s semiconductor industry acts as a major global economic tripwire.
Any blockade or occupation that disrupted advanced chip production would impose enormous costs not only on Taiwan, but on China and the wider global economy.
Taiwan also faces genuine vulnerabilities in energy resilience and maritime supply lines. Its agency therefore lies in raising the economic, military, and political costs of coercion.
By modernizing asymmetric military capabilities, reinforcing civic infrastructure, and deepening global economic interdependence, Taiwan can make aggression increasingly costly while strengthening its own resilience.
The goal is not to recreate an ancient battlefield trap. It is to ensure that coercion or invasion presents Beijing with costs that outweigh any conceivable benefit, preserving Taiwan’s freedom and democratic system.

articles.title: After Russia hits Kyiv’s Academy of Sciences with jet-powered drone, the Kremlin says Ukraine must “pay a price”
articles.body:
Russia says it is punishing Ukraine, and it is not hiding it. Dmitry Peskov, Kremlin spokesperson, says Ukraine must "pay a price" for its actions in recent months and calls Russia's intensified strikes "part of this price," according to UNIAN, citing Russian media.
Russia rarely admits its strikes are meant to punish a country rather than hit military targets, but Peskov did just that, casting the wave of attacks on Ukraine, which have struck apartment blocks, trains, and this week Kyiv's Academy of Sciences, as a "price" Ukraine has to pay. In the Kremlin's telling, Ukraine is being punished for its own deep strikes inside Russia.
Moscow calls the strikes a 'price'
Asked how Ukraine's strikes had affected Russia's position on peace talks, Peskov says Ukraine "will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months," adding, "This is what is happening now."
Russia, he says, must ensure "no one gets the idea to announce plans to inflict devastating strikes on it."
Kyiv's deep strikes draw the reprisal
The "actions" are Ukraine's strikes deep in the Russian rear, targeting its assets, helping it to fund the war. Russian President Vladimir Putin complained last week of a large Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow during Russia's parliamentary election and a June strike on St. Petersburg during an economic forum, Reuters reported.
Ukraine has also battered Russian refineries with long-range drones and missiles, cutting fuel output enough to spark shortages and force Moscow to curb exports and buy fuel abroad.
The price falls on civilians
What the Kremlin calls a price has fallen largely on Ukrainian civilians. Through September, Russian strikes have hit trains, data centers, gas stations, and educational institutions, and on 28 September, a drone set fire to the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv as people inside fled through the windows.

articles.title: Local representatives question official accounts after suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford
articles.body:
An MP and councillors representing the residents of the village near RAF Fairford who were evacuated due to a suspected terror plot have expressed scepticism and concern over the security response to threats made by Iran.
About 85 properties in Whelford, Gloucestershire, were evacuated on Sunday morning after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences in the village. The men, who were later re-arrested on suspicion of terror offences, were released on bail on Monday.
It is understood some residents were returning to their properties late on Monday, but a cordon remains around the village.
As speculation mounted over the circumstances surrounding the incident, concerns emerged about how events were handled by the authorities. In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.
However, it remains unclear who or what was behind the alleged activity. Iran has denied any involvement. Tehran’s embassy in London condemned what it described as “unfounded and malicious speculation” linking the country to the incident in the vicinity of the military base in Gloucestershire.
Roz Savage, the MP for South Cotswolds, said she had many questions about the circumstances of how the alleged terror plot was averted.
The Liberal Democrat MP, whose constituency covers the military base, said she would be writing to the prime minister and the defence secretary with her concerns.
“Ever since it was first announced six months ago that RAF Fairford was going to be used as the base for US military airstrikes on Iran, I’ve been asking questions of the government about whether they can assure my residents, my constituents, of their safety,” she said.
“They had given that assurance. However, I feel that the events of this weekend do cast that into doubt.”
She went on: “Who knew what? When did they know it? Where was the ball dropped? What more could have been done to secure the safety and security of my constituents?
“We are already in the process of writing to the secretary of state for defence and to the prime minister to try and ascertain the answers to some of these questions.”
There have been conflicting statements about who knew what and when. A farmer from Whelford told reporters she called police in the early hours of Sunday to report suspicious activity – which then triggered a rapid response.
But the US president, Donald Trump, also suggested to reporters the men had been under surveillance. Now, the men have been released on police bail.
Tristan Wilkinson, a cabinet member for Cotswold district council and councillor for the Lechlade, Kempsford and Fairford South ward, which covers Whelford, said: “The American president indicated last night in front of journalists that there was some intelligence and that these individuals were under surveillance.
“If that was to be true, that they would have been allowed to get so close to the base and drive what was, at the time, believed to be bombs into residential areas of a small village, I can’t imagine the security services allowing that to happen.
“I would have expected them to have done a hard stop on the van before they got to people’s homes. So that that doesn’t feel right.
“It seems insane that this appears to have been a tipoff from a member of the public, and the security services are claiming that there was a level of intelligence involved as well. I don’t see how those two things can both come through at the same time.”
He went on: “Back in July, the Iranians issued a statement saying that any countries that were providing military and practical support for the American effort were legitimate targets and at the time they named RAF Fairford specifically.
“So at that time, I and other civic leaders were calling for a more visible police presence to reassure residents, and that did happen.
“So from July, if you were around the base, you would have seen more police patrols.
“So if you’d parked a car up in a layby or somewhere near the base in the last few weeks, then you probably would have had the police contacting someone quickly to find out who you are and what you are doing.
“But I do think there’s been an increase in police presence in the last week as well. So I went past the base last Monday and I noticed that the non-manned entrances to the base have been fortified with vehicles.
“They put diggers and heavy vehicles in place that I’ve never seen before. So that’s quite an unusual step to block an emergency exit. So that led to speculation that maybe there was an increased level of concern from the base for them to use those measures.
“I wouldn’t expect the RAF to give a running commentary,” he added. “However, I think there’s always room for improvement. We have a significant military presence surrounded on three sides by residential housing. You can walk right up to the perimeter fence. There’s lots of military bases around the world that are quite remote for good reasons. So, the reality is this is a big military presence in a rural community.
“I will be asking for us to look at ways at how we can improve ongoing relations, and it’s not just relating to security matters. You know, we have other issues that you know with regard to flooding and noise, so there’s always more we can do.”

Russian intelligence services have significantly intensified efforts to create fake websites and social media pages that clone official Ukrainian government institutions and domestic media outlets, according to a warning issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) on September 28.
The SBU reported that these counterfeit platforms are being deployed in coordinated information-psychological operations (IPSO) to destabilize Ukraine’s domestic socio-political situation and erode its standing on the international stage.

articles.title: Russia keeps attacking Ukrainian data centers, calling it a ‘mandatory digital detox’
articles.body:
Russia keeps attacking Ukrainian data centers, calling it a ‘mandatory digital detox’
Russian forces continue to strike Ukrainian data centers. On September 25, they attacked an office building in Kyiv that houses a Datagroup data center. The center was damaged, but the company said all its services continued to run from backup sites.
On September 26, a Cosmonova data center in another Kyiv office building was hit. It had to shut down, interrupting broadcasts by several television channels. The strikes on data centers also left some Kyiv residents without internet access.
On September 28, a Russian drone struck an office building in Dnipro. The regional administration reported damage and casualties but did not say which companies occupied the building. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko also reported a strike on an office building in the city’s Shevchenkivskyi district overnight on September 28. Later that day, a strike on Kyiv set a National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine building on fire. A Ukrtelecom office and the German Embassy building are nearby.
On September 26, Russia’s Defense Ministry said it was striking data centers because they “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.” The next day, the ministry posted an image of a drone on social media with the caption “Digital detox” and the comment “Mandatory!”
Commenting on the data center strikes, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi said: “All infrastructure is at risk. That was true before, it is true now, and it will remain true until the war ends” (as quoted by RBC-Ukraine). He said the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief had already discussed protecting data centers and keeping mobile communications running.
Koretskyi said the authorities were doing everything they could to keep people connected, from protecting facilities directly to finding “unconventional solutions.” But, he said, in building a system to protect communications infrastructure, “we need to plan for the worst-case scenario and prepare accordingly.”

Russian forces struck Kyiv throughout the past week. Every day, city authorities and Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported casualties and destruction. These photographs show the aftermath of Russian strikes on Kyiv on the morning of September 28.

articles.title: Pope urges Russia, Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end war
articles.body:
Pope Leo urges Russia, Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end war
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT - Pope Leo on Sept 28 urged Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end their four-year war, hours after he had urged European leaders seeking to end conflicts to make concessions to achieve peace.
The first US pope also decried national leaders who he said are “beginning to speak about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming ever more destructive,” addressing a press conference aboard his flight to Rome after a four-day trip to France.
Leo said the Catholic Church has an obligation to call for peace and respect of human life.
“The Church has a responsibility to promote these values, continually inviting leaders — from Russia and Ukraine, as well as other countries — to come together, sit down, engage in dialogue,” said the pope.
He said leaders must “seek ways to solve problems without continuing these wars, which no longer make sense.”
“This is not about being political or non-political, but there needs to be a voice that seeks to promote the values of human dignity, the importance of life, and the possibility of perhaps spending more on health and education and less on weapons,” said Leo.
Earlier on Sept 28, the pope said Europe must be willing to sacrifice some positions to achieve peace in a speech in Metz, France, where he laid out his clearest vision yet for the future of the continent. REUTERS

articles.title: Beyond melodrama: Khajepasha on war, childhood and duty of Iranian cinema
articles.body:
Beyond melodrama: Khajepasha on war, childhood and duty of Iranian cinema
TEHRAN- Iranian filmmaker Babak Khajepasha believes cinema should do more than portray suffering. For him, a film dealing with war, the death of children, or a social tragedy should leave audiences with questions rather than simply tears.
Khajepasha, whose “In the Arms of the Tree” was selected as Iran’s submission for the 2025 Academy Awards, has repeatedly turned to children and family in his films. His latest feature, “The Land of Angels”, deals with children in Gaza. The film has also taken part in international events, including the Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival, where it received the Grand Prix for Best Feature Film. Khajepasha is also among the jury members of the 2026 BRICS+ International Film Festival in St. Petersburg.
In an interview with the Tehran Times, he spoke about the possibility of making a film on the recent tragedy in Minab, the difficulty of depicting the death of children without reducing cinema to melodrama, his decision to make films during the 40-day war, and what he saw during a recent visit to Hiroshima. He also discussed the international position of Iranian cinema, his earlier criticism of the Oscars and some major festivals, and why family remains one of the subjects he wants to pursue in his future work.
Looking beyond the tragedy
Speaking about the possibility of making a film about the tragedy in Minab, Khajepasha said he would be more interested in exploring the reasons behind such events than simply depicting their devastating consequences.
“The aspect that I, as a filmmaker, can enter and that deserves to be explored is the reason behind this tragedy,” he said, stressing that society should ask why it has been forced to experience such pain.
The filmmaker pointed to the loss of children in different parts of Iran, including Minab, Lamerd, Tabriz and Kermanshah during the recent war, saying that while addressing the suffering of children is important, cinema should also investigate why children repeatedly become victims of conflict and violence.
This concern, he explained, was also central to his research for “The Land of Angels”. During his research and conversations with Palestinians, he encountered stories that demonstrated the profound psychological impact of losing a child.
Khajepasha recalled speaking with a Palestinian father who had been holding his child when the child was killed. According to the filmmaker, the man later repeatedly returned to the same place, hoping that he too would be killed so that he could join his child. The father said he could not understand why he had been left alive.
For Khajepasha, such stories demonstrate that the killing of a child affects much more than the immediate victim. It leaves a psychological wound on the family and, ultimately, the wider community.
Yet he believes that cinema must be careful not to turn such suffering into an exercise in emotional manipulation.
From tears to questions
That is also why Khajepasha is wary of making films about war and children that rely entirely on emotion.
If simply seeing the suffering of children were enough to change the world's response to violence, he said, the many films and documentaries made about Gaza and other conflicts would already have brought about such a change.
“Just talking about how much pain we are in does not necessarily take us a step forward,” he said. “We have to look at this from an intellectual perspective. We have to search for its causes and ask where this pain is supposed to take us.”
For “The Land of Angels”, he wanted the audience to leave with a question.
A viewer may accept that there are fighters, a military conflict and casualties in a war, he explained. But the death of thousands of children should lead to another question: why are these children being killed?
That question, in his view, can open the door to wider discussions about the position of children in contemporary society, the pressures placed on them and even the declining importance attached to having children in some parts of the world.
Khajepasha prefers this kind of cinema to a film that simply asks its audience to cry.
“I don't want to make a film merely so that audiences cry,” he said. “We have to value the film itself. There have to be other reasons for making it.”
He pointed to techniques used in dramatic literature and epic theater, including distancing, which encourage audiences to think about a work instead of simply surrendering to its emotional effect. A film, he said, should stay with the viewer as a question after the screening.
When filmmaking becomes a duty
The same idea of responsibility was behind Khajepasha's decision to work during the 40-day War.
At the time, Tehran and other parts of the country were facing an extraordinary situation as they came under US and Zionist regime airstrikes. Khajepasha said he saw people from different professions doing more than their normal duties: bakers working additional shifts, doctors and nurses continuing their work in hospitals and other citizens finding ways to contribute.
For him and some of his colleagues, filmmaking became another form of service.
“Sometimes we make films because we are filmmakers. Sometimes, as Iranians, we have another national duty,” he said. “At that point, it is no longer simply about filmmaking. It is a form of service.”
Under ordinary circumstances, he acknowledged, starting a production so quickly and without the usual preparation would not have been logical. But he felt that the circumstances demanded a response.
“As someone working in the arts, I felt I had a responsibility,” he said. “My instrument is cinema and television.”
He began work only a few days after the war started and now looks back on the experience with particular satisfaction.
The reason, he explained, was not necessarily that the films were more successful than his other work. It was the feeling that he was doing something directly for his own people.
“I am happy that, during that period, instead of standing on the sidelines, I was able to take a step,” he said.
Hiroshima: between memory and spectacle
A recent trip to Hiroshima gave Khajepasha another opportunity to think about the way major human tragedies are remembered.
He attended the annual ceremony commemorating the victims of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and found the gathering visually striking and, from a filmmaker's perspective, fascinating. Yet he said the event left him with mixed feelings.
The scale of the tragedy, he argued, seemed much greater than what was being conveyed by the ceremony.
“I felt that, instead of the truth being fully expressed, I was watching more of a show,” he said.
Khajepasha extended that observation to the way peace is sometimes represented internationally. He questioned the gap that can exist between institutions and governments that publicly promote peace and countries whose policies have contributed to conflicts elsewhere.
But his experience in Japan did not leave him simply pessimistic. He said he encountered ordinary people who appeared genuinely concerned about events beyond their own borders.
When some Japanese people learned that he was Iranian, he recalled, they immediately brought up the victims of the recent tragedy in Minab and other Iranian victims.
He said he had encountered similar reactions in other countries and believes that ordinary people may ultimately understand such tragedies more deeply than political rhetoric suggests.
Iranian cinema and the international festival circuit
Khajepasha also returned to comments he made while “In the Arms of the Tree” was Iran's Oscar submission. At the time, he had questioned whether artistic quality alone determines a film's international success.
His criticism, he explained, was not simply about whether his own film would advance in the Oscar race. He was talking about the broader position of art and cinema.
In his view, political considerations, lobbying and relationships can influence some major international cultural institutions. He also believes that the influence of politics has become particularly visible in some film festivals.
That does not mean he considers the entire international festival circuit politicized.
He mentioned festivals held in South Korea, Morocco, Egypt, Armenia, Russia and Turkey among festivals that continue to offer valuable platforms for filmmakers. Iranian cinema, he stressed, has also received genuine international recognition through films by directors such as Asghar Farhadi and Majid Majidi.
The quality of an individual film, he argued, should not be reduced to the festival at which it appears or the prize it receives.
“A festival award alone cannot determine the value of a film,” he said.
He also believes filmmakers themselves have a responsibility not to allow the desire for international recognition to dictate their artistic choices.
Family at the center
Children feature prominently in both “In the Arms of the Tree” and “The Land of Angels”, but Khajepasha does not see himself primarily as a filmmaker of children's stories.
His deeper interest, he said, is the family.
He usually tries to include children in his films because their presence gives the story another dimension, but he would like to explore the family itself more extensively in future work.
“I would like to make more films about the family itself,” he said, describing it as one of the most important and vulnerable foundations of human societies.
He believes the issue has particular importance in Iran because family relationships are deeply connected to the country's cultural identity.
Iran cannot simply reproduce changes that have taken place in other societies, he argued. Relationships among parents, children and extended family members have a particular cultural meaning in Iranian society.
For that reason, he believes Iranian cinema should address the pressures facing families instead of treating changes in family structures as inevitable.
‘First make a good film’
Khajepasha will soon have an opportunity to examine films from the other side of the filmmaking process, as a jury member of the BRICS+ International Film Festival in St. Petersburg.
At the time of the interview, the festival's films had not yet been sent to the jury, so he had not begun watching them. But he already knew what his first criterion would be.
The film itself comes first.
For Khajepasha, a film needs to have a sound story and plot as well as convincing cinematic elements such as mise-en-scène and visual language. A political or social message cannot make up for weaknesses in the filmmaking.
He is particularly critical of films that appear to have been made primarily to deliver a message.
“If we want to criticize a society, we first have to make a good film,” he said. “If we simply shout our message at the audience, the audience will realize immediately that the filmmaker has an agenda.”
The same principle applies to films carrying messages that he himself agrees with, he added.
“A good film that disagrees with our beliefs can sometimes be less damaging than a bad film that is trying to promote our beliefs,” he said.
As a juror, Khajepasha said his first priority would therefore be cinematic quality.
“Before a film can make an audience believe in its message, it has to make the audience believe in the film itself,” he concluded.
SAB/

articles.title: Russian drone strikes near Ukraine-Poland border crossing in Volyn Oblast
articles.body:
A Russian drone struck near the Yahodyn border crossing in Ukraine's Volyn Oblast, several hundred meters from the Polish border, Ukrainian and Polish officials said on Sept. 28.
Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the drone struck Ukrainian territory about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Dorohusk crossing and did not enter Polish airspace.
"Another Russian attack on western Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X. "There was no violation of Polish airspace. Our air defense systems and aircraft were ready for action."
Sources in Ukraine's State Border Guard Service told Ukrainska Pravda that the Russian attack drone struck several hundred meters from the border and did not damage the Yahodyn crossing itself.
Ukrainian monitoring channels reported Russian drones moving toward the Yahodyn border crossing during the afternoon of Sept. 28.
The strike follows a series of recent Russian attacks near the Polish border. On Sept. 17, a Russian drone came down near a gas station in Yahodyn.
Four days earlier, on Sept. 13, a Russian drone hit a truck about 800 meters (0.5 miles) from the Polish border near the same crossing. Russian forces also struck the locomotive of a passenger train traveling to Warsaw that day.
Incursions by Russian munitions into Polish airspace have also become increasingly frequent as Russia's war in Ukraine continues, prompting Poland to scramble military aircraft during attacks on western Ukraine.
Poland will change procedures for military aircraft and helicopters that engage objects entering from the direction of Russia, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Sept. 28.
Under the current peacetime procedure, Polish pilots must fly close enough to visually confirm a target in Polish airspace before firing at it.
The new procedures will replace this visual identification with so-called positive identification, meaning the radar reading alone will be enough for the pilot or the operational commander to authorize shooting down the object, Polish broadcaster RMF24 reported.

articles.title: Iran ready to say it will never develop nuclear weapons, Trump trumpets
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, September 28. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump says Iran is ready to state that it is not going to develop nuclear weapons.
"They’ll never have a nuclear weapon, and they understand that. And they're willing to say that," he told reporters.
Tehran has repeatedly stressed that it is not seeking to develop nuclear arms. Moreover, Western intelligence agencies have found no evidence of Iran developing nuclear weapons. The New York Times also confirmed this at the end of January. Additionally, a fatwa (religious edict) issued by the former supreme leader of the Islamic Republic, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has been in effect in Iran since 2003, prohibiting the production of nuclear weapons.
Trump said in August that Iran’s refusal from possessing nuclear weapons would be officially committed to paper. Last week, he said that a deal with Iran would be concluded after the midterm elections to the US Congress in November. Shortly after that, he said that the deal could be reached even before the election.

articles.title: Unfreezing Europe's Russian assets debate
articles.body:
Unfreezing Europe's Russian assets debate
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever meets with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni (not in picture) before their meeting at Palazzo Chigi on Sept. 7, 2026 in Rome, Italy. (Antonio Masiello/Getty Images)
There has been little movement in EU circles on the question of using over 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of immobilized Russian assets since Sweden reopened the topic a month ago, but those wanting to move the matter forward are increasingly going public with their ideas.
Months after the idea of directly using Russian assets was shot down in Brussels, Sweden led a new push on Aug. 27 to reopen the question as a way to deliver new support to Ukraine without hurting EU taxpayers and voters.
The idea was given a fresh sense of urgency with President Volodymyr Zelensky's claim that Kyiv faces a $27 billion hole in its budget for 2026, and because third countries have yet to step in to cover the remaining third of what Ukraine needs, not already paid for by the EU's 90 billion euro ($102 billion) support loan.
read also
But three European Commission officials told the Kyiv Independent that, despite Sweden's wish to push the issue through, it will not do so until there is a "clear instruction from the member states" on what they want.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first announced the plan to use Russian assets in her 2025 State of the Union speech, only to see it fall apart in the face of determined opposition, notably from Belgium.
National diplomats, for their part, have also not taken the initiative to formulate a clear proposal of their own, and Sweden has had a caretaker government since its Sept. 13 election, meaning less scope to lead the charge — for now.
Cue the think-tankers
Absent a push from EU governments themselves, the discussion is instead playing out in newspaper columns, and at think tank events.
Ex-British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak took to The Times newspaper to say that "using the frozen Russian assets would show Putin the steel he believes we lack," on Sept. 26.
He dismissed the nervousness of some about using them as "crippling, hyper-legalistic caution … increasingly absurd in a world in which EU airports are menaced by explosive-laden drones."
And at an event organized by the European Policy Center think tank on Sep. 28, Ukraine's Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko teamed up with financial commentator Hugo Dixon to try to persuade attendees of their proposed workarounds.
Marchenko said the EU should introduce a mechanism to shift custodianship of the Russian assets away from Belgium and its clearing house Euroclear, so that the legal risk is assumed by the EU as a whole, something he first called for in a Sept. 4 interview with Euronews.
Fellow panelist Dixon presented his website, The Russian Transfer, which includes a draft regulation that he said is "designed to take Belgium out of the line of fire," were the EU to adopt it.
It includes wording that would effectively bind the EU to reimburse any actor for any "loss, cost, or expense," incurred for transferring the assets to EU protection, as well as for retaliatory actions taken by Russia or on its behalf.
Dixon argued that his proposal is an improvement on the European Commission's December proposal, which entailed the EU borrowing money from Euroclear, because that required a line of liquidity to cover the full amount, which did not exist.
While such a wording could potentially compensate for Russia successfully pressuring friendly jurisdictions to seize Belgian assets in third countries, that scenario still remains unlikely to most.
The greater financial risk is lost business opportunities for Euroclear from countries less democratic than the EU.
Investors "economically see it (the transferring of assets away from Euroclear) as a confiscation," said Wim Schoutens, a finance professor at the Belgian university, KU Leuven.
He argued on the panel that their perception and trust in markets matters, and that such moves could lead to long-term damage.
If a state fears that the EU could appropriate its assets in the future, the argument goes that it is more likely to keep them outside the EU's jurisdiction from the outset, and thus Euroclear, in particular, loses business.
And so long as Belgium maintains a Bilateral Investment Treaty with Russia, there remains a vehicle that the Russian Central Bank could theoretically use to challenge any transfer of its assets from Euroclear.
Compromis à la Belge
In addition to shielding Euroclear from legal and financial risks and sharing the burden of potential lawsuits, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever previously said he would not be able to support using immobilized Russian assets without commitments from other countries holding such assets to also take action.
Other significant holders of assets are Japan, the U.K., France, Canada, Luxembourg, Switzerland, and the U.S., in that order.
Two EU officials with knowledge of the negotiations over the Russian assets in 2025 said that on the technical level, Belgian and EU experts were "seeing eye to eye," on the outlines of a potential deal, but that the matter had remained stuck at the political level.
And there is little to suggest that political deadlock has been resolved.
On Sept. 2, Luxembourg's Foreign Minister Xavier Bettel told journalists "I am still waiting for the solidarity mechanism," but complained that when the topic is broached, he finds some leaders "burying their heads in the sand, like ostriches."
This raises the question of whether there remain other, underexplored options for the EU to support Ukraine without directly using its assets.
Another think tank, the Center for Development Finance Studies, believes it has such an idea: the Windfall Optimization Loan Framework, or WOLF.
The think tank's director, Thomas Venon, shared in an interview with the Kyiv Independent that his career in the finance industry taught him "if you want something to work, keep the innovation to an absolute minimum."
For him, the EU has already taken two innovative steps, which pave the way for another use of the Russian assets, namely to generate a new loan using the interest they accumulate.
The G7's agreement in 2024 to use interest generated on Russia's immobilized assets to provide Ukraine a 45 billion euro loan already set a precedent for Venon's idea, but he argues that a much better-performing loan could be created.
To make that happen, the WOLF would entail the EU agreeing to immobilize Russia's assets for a fixed (long) time, such as 15-20 years, instead of the "indefinite" freeze in place now, which could theoretically be undone at any time, if the EU decides to do so.
Venon argues that a specific time frame helps attract financiers to back the loan, because there is in-built certainty over the timespan of the loan, and that the EU"s agreement in December 2025 to immobilize Russia's assets indefinitely already showed the bloc is able to think in a longer-term.
The only thing left to be done, in Venon's view, would be for the EU to instruct Euroclear to invest the Russian assets like it was doing before they were immobilized.
Since then, Euroclear has essentially taken a hands-off approach to those assets, but that means the income generated from them could be much higher.
"90 billion euros with a 20-year freeze could be realistic," Venon said.
And creating this loan could be "strategically wise," Venon argues, as it leaves the assets intact for another decision later on, if needed.
One senior EU official familiar with the negotiations around using Russian assets said "the formula can work if all member states agree," but they were not sure of the precise amount the WOLF could generate as a new loan.
And two national ambassadors agreed the idea could work, as an alternative to simply using the assets as a whole, for which they doubt there is enough political will.
"Theoretically speaking, it's possible," Marchenko said at the event, when asked if a new, higher-yielding version of the G7 loan could work.
"But then you introduce market risk," Schoutens said.
"If it pays out, four, five, or six percent, this is fine. But if not, who is going to make up the losses?" he asked.
Ultimately, for any idea from any think tank to gain traction, it needs to be wholeheartedly embraced by an EU country, who will gather consensus around it.

articles.title: Denmark buys Ukrainian-founded firm’s ground drones
articles.body:
- Denmark bought nine Dropla 4x4 unmanned ground vehicles to train drone operators, including conscripts, at the Danish Defence Drone Center.
- The vehicles were delivered without weapon mounts, and Denmark is studying adding remote weapon stations and communications equipment.
Denmark’s armed forces have taken delivery of nine unmanned ground vehicles built by Dropla, a Danish company founded by Ukrainians, to train drone operators, including conscripts, at the country’s military drone center.
Denmark’s defense procurement agency, known by its Danish initials FMI, bought the Dropla 4×4 vehicles for the Danish Defence Drone Center, the agency said Sept. 28. An unmanned ground vehicle, or UGV, is a vehicle that drives itself or is steered remotely with no crew aboard. The agency did not disclose the price of the order or when the vehicles arrived.
The Danish version of the Dropla 4×4 was delivered without a weapon mount. FMI said it is already studying how to fit the vehicles with extra equipment such as a remotely operated weapon station, which lets a soldier aim and fire a machine gun from a safe distance, and new communications gear. The agency said those plans draw on lessons from the war in Ukraine and on its own trials of other UGVs in Denmark.
Colonel Thomas Øgendahl Knudsen, who heads FMI’s land division, said unmanned systems are developing quickly, so the Danish military needs to build experience with them and bring them into soldier training now. He said the new vehicles let the drone center work with ground drones while exploring how the technology could be used across the armed forces in the future.
The purchase is FMI’s second batch of UGVs this year. Earlier in 2026, the agency bought eight unmanned ground vehicles for the Danish Army, which FMI said have since been tested in a range of operational scenarios with strong results.
Dropla Tech was founded in 2023 by four Ukrainian entrepreneurs and is headquartered in Odense, Denmark, with its engineering and operations teams working in Ukraine. The company is best known for Blue Eyes, an artificial intelligence system that detects mines, improvised explosive devices and loitering drones without needing a cloud connection. Dropla says the system has confirmed more than 5,000 explosive threats in Ukraine.
The company builds two modular UGV platforms, the Dropla 4×4 and Dropla 6×6. Both can be configured for casualty evacuation, cargo delivery, reconnaissance, remote weapon stations and counter-drone missions. Dropla has also signed an agreement with Ukrainian company Frontline Robotics to integrate its Burya weapon turret onto the vehicles.
The Danish military has worked with Dropla before. During a six-month innovation project that ended this summer, the armed forces tested a Dropla prototype built for evacuation and logistics. That vehicle started out with four wheels but was fitted with two more on the military’s recommendation to make it more stable.
Dropla raised €2.4 million ($2.7 million) in 2025 from investors including Denmark’s state Export and Investment Fund, and in July 2026 it received an undisclosed investment from U.S.-Ukrainian group MITS Capital. The company says it wants to scale production to as many as 3,000 UGVs a year.

articles.title: Iran nearing completion of key rail link key for India’s gateway to Eurasia
articles.body:
Iran nearing completion of key rail link key for India’s gateway to Eurasia
Iran has completed laying track on the southern stretch of the Chabahar-Zahedan railway, closing a key gap in a route designed to connect the port of Chabahar on the Gulf of Oman to Zahedan near the Afghan border. 
Iranian railway official Abbas Khatibi said last week that tracks had been laid for the crucial 480km stretch between Chabahar and Khash, and currently the priority is to complete the stations on the route, Tasnim news agency reported. 
The Chabahar–Zahedan link stretches 630 km, or 735 km including branch lines. With the northern sections already linked to the existing rail network, the Iranian authorities are now preparing it for operation. 
The Chabahar–Zahedan link is an extension of the larger International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC), backed by India, Iran and Russia. The project has been in the making for decades because of its huge infrastructure requirements and has also been slowed by Western sanctions on both Iran and Russia. 
The milestone comes as the Middle East conflict has disrupted traditional transport and energy routes across the region. Chabahar has direct access to the Indian Ocean without requiring ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a major chokepoint affected by the conflict.
Strategic Step: Iran Completes Chabahar-Zahedan Rail Link – Connecting Central Asia to Indian Ocean
The major infrastructure project looks set to become fully operational within 3-4 months with final safety checks for the route underway. (Economic Times)
The route connects… pic.twitter.com/pUKsSzJEJq
For India, the Chabahar-Zahedan link strengthens a trade route that reaches Afghanistan and Central Asia without transiting Pakistan. Cargo arriving by sea at Chabahar would be able to move inland through Iran’s rail and road network toward landlocked regional markets. 
India’s role in Chabahar is complicated by US sanctions. A conditional waiver covering the project, in which India invested around $120 million, expired in April. New Delhi maintained it was discussing the issue with both Tehran and Washington, describing the regional conflict as a “complicating factor.” 
In July, the conflict touched Chabahar itself, when US forces struck a surveillance tower at the neighboring Shahid Kalantari terminal linked to the project. India said the terminal was not damaged.

articles.title: Trump's Taxpayer-Funded Ads Draw Bipartisan Criticism
articles.body:
President Donald Trump declares that “this is the final battle” in one of several taxpayer-funded television ads airing ahead of November’s midterm elections, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the spots violate federal law.
The 30-second ad is a black-and-white video of Trump walking down a hall over audio of his warnings against “the deep state,” “warmongers,” “globalists,” “Marxists,” “communists,” and “fascists.”
Trump posted the same video on his Truth Social platform in 2023, but with one difference: Then, the monochromatic ad ended with words on screen calling on the viewer to join Trump’s campaign and fine print saying it was “Paid for by Donald J. Trump for President 2024, Inc.” This time, the 2026 ad says at the bottom: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
CNN reported that the ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday. CNBC also reported that the ad aired during Fox News Sunday, citing data from advertising intelligence company AdImpact, adding that the TV ad has cost more than $362,000 so far.
A second advert with the same “paid for by the U.S. government” disclaimer began airing on Wednesday. The ad, which featured the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN, showed a montage of photos and videos of Trump, intercut with campaign talking points like “largest tax cuts in history” and “reigniting American manufacturing.” This ad, which CNBC reported also aired over the weekend, citing AdImpact data, has cost the federal government nearly $920,000 to date. It also apparently did not get the approval of JMSN, who posted on social media that he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”
A third, which is a minute long, features scenic views of Mount Rushmore interspersed with parts of Trump’s speech there for the Fourth of July anniversary.
The ads appear to be part of a campaign blitz ahead of the November midterms, in which the GOP is hoping to defend its majorities in Congress.
Some lawmakers, including from his own Republican Party, are raising concerns with Trump and the White House over the advertisements. Asked about the ads by CBS News on Sunday, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said: “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves.” (Kennedy was referring to former Homeland Security Secretary Noem, who came under fire for spending $220 million on an advertising campaign for border security.)
When asked about the “Love Me” ad, Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said that the use of taxpayer money was reminiscent of the far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. “It’s inappropriate,” Tillis told reporters.
Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican and a vocal Trump critic, posted on social media about the “Final Battle” ad: “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics.”
Democrats also raised questions. In a Sept. 24 letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire demanded answers on the “Love Me” ad’s production cost, the agencies and external contractors involved, the source of funds, and the legal and ethical bases for the spot. Hassan wrote in her letter that the ad “does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions.” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey posted to social media about the black-and-white clip: “How much taxpayer money did the government spend on this ad?”
In another Sept. 24 letter, congressional Democrats on appropriations panels wrote to the White House that the “Love Me” ad should be taken off the air, as it was “the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars.”
But the White House has defended the ads—which it called, in a Sept. 25 press release, “public service announcements.” A White House official told TIME Friday that the ads weren’t political, didn’t have a call to action, and that the President wasn't on the ballot.
A spokesperson instead said that the ads were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
What does the law say?
Since the 1950s, yearly funding bills—including the appropriations measure the President recently signed—routinely ban the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda.”
The Government Accountability Office, which investigates how appropriated funds are spent, has interpreted this to refer to material that is “purely partisan,” “self-aggrandizing,” or “covert.” But it also noted that administrations may need to advocate or defend their policies.
Some lawmakers have pointed to potential violations of the Hatch Act, the 1939 act that limits the political activities of federal civilian employees in the executive branch. The President is exempt from the Hatch Act, though some argue that White House employees who facilitated the airing of the ads aren’t. Last week, the non-profit advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint before the GAO and the Office of Special Counsel, which is responsible for overseeing Hatch Act violations, seeking investigation and enforcement of relevant laws.
In defense of the “public service announcements,” the White House has pointed to previous ad campaigns during the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden. (During the Bush Administration, one campaign did violate the anti-propaganda measure.)
“When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called ‘public education,’” the Trump White House said. “When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it ‘propaganda.’”

articles.title: Liminal’s mass-producible UGV heads to Pentagon trial
articles.body:
- Liminal Industries advanced to Phase II of GroundBreaker 1 and will demonstrate its DUEL-V unmanned ground vehicle at Camp Grafton, North Dakota, in mid-October.
- Companies that perform well may be invited to propose for a prototype Other Transaction Agreement award.
Liminal Industries, a U.S. startup building unmanned ground vehicles meant to be produced and fielded in large numbers, has advanced to the second phase of the GroundBreaker 1 competition and will demonstrate its DUEL-V vehicle to U.S. military evaluators in North Dakota next month.
The company announced Sept. 28 that its Phase I submission passed technical evaluation and that it will bring multiple DUEL-V vehicles to Camp Grafton in mid-October. An unmanned ground vehicle, or UGV, is a vehicle that operates on land with no crew aboard, driven by a remote operator or by its own software.
DUEL-V, short for Dynamic Unmanned Expendable Light Vehicle, is a compact, remotely operated platform that Liminal designed around three priorities: low cost, adaptability and the ability to build it at scale. It uses a modular layout that accepts different mission payloads, runs on four-wheel drive and can operate in either orientation. The company has not released its size, weight, speed, range, payload capacity or price.
“Scale has been a design requirement from the beginning,” said Bradley Balzer, founder and CEO of Liminal Industries. “Cost, manufacturing, and operator usability determine whether a ground system can become a widely deployed capability. GroundBreaker gives us an opportunity to demonstrate that approach and put DUEL-V in front of the people who will shape its deployment at scale.”
Liminal says its development relies on field testing, feedback from operators and rapid hardware changes between versions. It first unveiled DUEL-V on Oct. 14, 2025, when Balzer pitched it as the ground equivalent of an FPV drone, the cheap first-person-view quadcopters that armies in Ukraine now use by the hundreds of thousands. At the time, the company did not disclose payload options, how much the vehicle can drive itself or whether it can keep working under electronic jamming, and it has not released those details since.
GroundBreaker 1 is a joint Department of War demonstration meant to speed up the military’s adoption of unmanned ground vehicles. U.S. Army Contracting Command issued the call for white papers on Aug. 21 through the Department of War Drone OTA Consortium, which limited the competition to companies already enrolled in that consortium. Government teams from the Office of the Secretary of War and the military services are supporting the event.
The U.S. Army is looking for complete systems that troops can use in both combat and non-combat settings. The solicitation lists missions including reconnaissance and surveillance, tactical logistics, explosive ordnance disposal and route clearance, search and rescue, and force protection. White papers were scored out of 100 points: 40% for technical merit and design, 35% for readiness to deliver and demonstrate, 15% for cost and affordability, and 10% for past performance. The recommended threshold to reach Phase II was 75 points.
At Camp Grafton, service members will operate the vehicles in realistic field conditions and give feedback on how easy they are to use and how well they perform their missions. Companies will also make live pitches to government evaluators. Vendors whose vehicles show “high tactical value and technical maturity” may then be invited to submit a full technical and cost proposal for a prototype Other Transaction Agreement, a contract type the Pentagon uses to buy and test new technology faster than through traditional procurement.
GroundBreaker follows the demonstration-first model of the Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program, which runs aerial drones through competitive “Gauntlet” trials before placing large orders. The department has not said how many UGVs it plans to buy after GroundBreaker 1 or how many companies will take part in the October event.
